title: Build an MCP client
content: If you see: Errno::ENOENT: Check your server path and ensure the command (ruby, python3, node) is available Connection refused: Ensure the server is running and the path is correct Tool execution failed: Verify the tool’s required environment variables are set Anthropic::Errors::AuthenticationError: Check your .env file has a valid ANTHROPIC_API_KEY [Stopped after 10 tool-use turns]: Claude kept asking for tools, so the client stopped at MAX_TOOL_TURNS and returned the text collected so far You can find the complete code for this tutorial here.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Before starting, ensure your system meets these requirements: Rust and Cargo 1.88 or newer Anthropic API key (Claude) A Python, Node.js, or executable MCP server to connect to

title: Build an MCP client
content: First, create a new Rust project: cargo new mcp-client-rust cd mcp-client-rust Replace the contents of Cargo.toml with the following: Cargo.toml [package] name = "mcp-client-rust" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2024" [dependencies] anyhow = "1.0.104" jsonschema = "0.59" # Only the client half of rmcp is needed, over a child-process stdio transport. rmcp = { version = "3.4", features = [ "client", "transport-io", "transport-child-process", ], default-features = false } # The Messages API is called directly, which keeps the provider's content # blocks verbatim. That matters for signed thinking blocks; see request_model. reqwest = { version = "0.13", features = ["json"] } serde = { version = "1.0", features = ["derive"] } serde_json = "1.0.151" tokio = { version = "1.53", features = ["full"] } dotenvy = "0.15.7" The rmcp crate provides the Rust MCP SDK and the child-process stdio transport. Only its client half is enabled. The client calls the Messages API directly with reqwest. Calling the API directly keeps the content blocks of each reply verbatim, which matters when a reply contains a signed thinking block. The jsonschema crate validates structured tool results against the schema a tool declares.

title: Build an MCP client
content: You’ll need an Anthropic API key from the Anthropic Console.Create a .env file to store it: echo "ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-api-key-goes-here" > .env Add .env to your .gitignore: echo ".env" >> .gitignore The client loads .env when the file exists. Exporting ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the shell works as well. Make sure you keep your ANTHROPIC_API_KEY secure!

title: Build an MCP client
content: Open src/main.rs and replace its contents as you work through the following sections.

title: Build an MCP client
content: First, add the imports and constants: use anyhow::{Context, Result, bail}; use jsonschema::Validator; use rmcp::model::{ CallToolRequestParams, CallToolResult, ClientCapabilities, ClientConfig, Implementation, ProtocolVersion, Tool as McpTool, }; use rmcp::service::{ClientLifecycleMode, ClientServiceExt, RoleClient, RunningService}; use rmcp::transport::TokioChildProcess; use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize}; use serde_json::{Value, json}; use std::collections::HashMap; use std::time::Duration; use tokio::io::{self, AsyncBufReadExt, BufReader}; use tokio::process::Command; const MODEL_ANTHROPIC: &str = "claude-opus-5"; /// The model may think before answering, and max_tokens caps thinking /// plus the reply, so leave room for both. const MAX_TOKENS: u32 = 10000; const MAX_TOOL_TURNS: usize = 10; const ANTHROPIC_API_BASE: &str = "https://api.anthropic.com"; const ANTHROPIC_VERSION: &str = "2023-06-01"; const REQUEST_TIMEOUT: Duration = Duration::from_secs(120); MAX_TOKENS caps the thinking and the reply together. MAX_TOOL_TURNS bounds how many rounds of tool calls one query may take. REQUEST_TIMEOUT applies to each request sent to the Messages API.Next, add the types for the Messages API and the client structure: /// One turn of the conversation, as the Messages API takes it. /// /// `content` is a list of raw blocks rather than typed ones on purpose. An /// assistant turn is fed straight back on the next request, and Claude requires /// the blocks it sent to return unchanged -- a thinking block's `signature` /// included. Reserialising through a narrower type would drop whatever it does /// not model. #[derive(Serialize, Clone)] struct Message { role: &'static str, content: Vec<Value>, } impl Message { fn user(content: Vec<Value>) -> Self { Message { role: "user", content, } } fn assistant(content: Vec<Value>) -> Self { Message { role: "assistant", content, } } } /// A tool as the Messages API declares it, converted from an MCP tool. #[derive(Serialize, Clone)]

title: Build an MCP client
content: Clone)] struct ToolDefinition { name: String, #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")] description: Option<String>, input_schema: Value, } #[derive(Serialize)] struct MessagesRequest<'a> { model: &'a str, max_tokens: u32, messages: &'a [Message], tools: &'a [ToolDefinition], } #[derive(Deserialize)] struct MessagesResponse { content: Vec<Value>, } /// The `type` of a content block, when it has one. fn block_type(block: &Value) -> &str { block .get("type") .and_then(Value::as_str) .unwrap_or_default() } struct MCPClient { http: reqwest::Client, session: Option<RunningService<RoleClient, ClientConfig>>, tools: Vec<ToolDefinition>, /// Compiled `outputSchema` per tool name. rmcp does not validate results, /// so this client does it with the `jsonschema` crate. output_schemas: HashMap<String, Validator>, } Message holds the content blocks of one turn as raw serde_json::Values. An assistant turn goes back to the API unchanged on the next request, with any thinking block and its signature intact. ToolDefinition is a tool as the Messages API declares it. MCPClient keeps the HTTP client, the active MCP session, the tools in Messages API form, and one compiled validator per tool that declares an outputSchema.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Next, open the impl MCPClient block with the constructor. The methods in the following sections go inside this block, which closes after cleanup: impl MCPClient { fn new() -> Result<Self> { Ok(MCPClient { http: reqwest::Client::builder() .timeout(REQUEST_TIMEOUT) .build() .context("Failed to build HTTP client")?, session: None, tools: Vec::new(), output_schemas: HashMap::new(), }) } new builds a reqwest::Client with the request timeout. The API key is read later, when a request is sent, so connecting to a server and listing its tools works without one.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Add this method inside the impl MCPClient block: /// Check a result against its tool's declared `outputSchema`. Error results /// are exempt: they carry a message, not data. fn validate_tool_output(&self, name: &str, result: &CallToolResult) -> Result<()> { let Some(validator) = self.output_schemas.get(name) else { return Ok(()); }; if result.is_error.unwrap_or(false) { return Ok(()); } let Some(structured) = &result.structured_content else { bail!("Tool {name} declares an output schema but returned no structured content"); }; if let Err(error) = validator.validate(structured) { bail!("Structured content from tool {name} does not match its output schema: {error}"); } Ok(()) } A tool may declare an outputSchema, and the specification asks clients to validate structuredContent against it. rmcp does not do this, so the client keeps a compiled jsonschema::Validator per tool and checks each successful result. A result with is_error set carries a message, so it is exempt. A tool that declares a schema and returns no structured content is reported as an error.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Add this method inside the impl MCPClient block: async fn connect_to_server(&mut self, server_args: &[String]) -> Result<()> { if self.session.is_some() { bail!("Client is already connected to a server"); } let mut command = Command::new(&server_args[0]); command.args(&server_args[1..]); let process = TokioChildProcess::new(command) .with_context(|| format!("Failed to spawn server process for {:?}", server_args))?; // Without a ClientConfig the client would report rmcp's own crate name // and version rather than its own. let config = ClientConfig::new( ClientCapabilities::default(), Implementation::new("mcp-client-rust", "1.0.0"), ); // `Auto` probes server/discover and falls back to the 2025-11-25 // initialize handshake, matching the Python and TypeScript clients. // `serve` alone would only ever do the legacy handshake, under which a // server cannot offer this era's features -- an array-rooted // `outputSchema`, for one, which get_alerts uses. let session = config .serve_with_lifecycle( process, ClientLifecycleMode::Auto { preferred_versions: vec![ProtocolVersion::V_2026_07_28], legacy_version: Some(ProtocolVersion::V_2025_11_25), }, ) .await?; let rmcp_tools = session .list_all_tools() .await .context("Unable to list tools from server")?; let tool_names: Vec<String> = rmcp_tools .iter() .map(|tool| tool.name.to_string()) .collect(); let protocol_version = session .peer_info() .map(|info| info.protocol_version.to_string()) .unwrap_or_else(|| "unknown".to_string()); println!("Connected over protocol {protocol_version} with tools: {tool_names:?}"); // An outputSchema root may be any JSON Schema, not just an object. for tool in &rmcp_tools { let Some(schema) = &tool.output_schema else { continue; }; let schema = Value::Object(schema.as_ref().clone()); let validator = Validator::new(&schema).with_context(|| { format!("Failed to compile output schema of tool {}", tool.name) })?; self.output_schemas.insert(tool.name.to_string(), validator); } self.tools =

title: Build an MCP client
content: = convert_tools(&rmcp_tools); self.session = Some(session); Ok(()) } This method: Starts the server as a child process using the command and arguments supplied on the command line Names the client mcp-client-rust through a ClientConfig Negotiates the protocol with serve_with_lifecycle and ClientLifecycleMode::Auto, which probes server/discover for 2026-07-28 and falls back to the 2025-11-25 initialize handshake Lists all tools advertised by the server and prints the negotiated protocol version with the tool names Compiles a validator from each tool’s outputSchema Converts the tools into the form used in model requests rmcp’s serve method alone performs only the legacy handshake. The Auto mode makes the features of the current revision reachable, including an outputSchema whose root is an array.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Now add the core query-processing method inside impl MCPClient: async fn process_query(&mut self, query: &str) -> Result<String> { let session = self .session .as_ref() .context("Client is not connected to any server")?; let mut messages = vec![Message::user(vec![json!({"type": "text", "text": query})])]; let mut final_text = Vec::new(); // Initial Claude API call with tools let mut content = self.request_model(&messages).await?; // Keep calling tools until Claude answers without one, up to a cap. for _ in 0..MAX_TOOL_TURNS { let mut tool_uses = Vec::new(); for block in &content { match block_type(block) { "text" => { if let Some(text) = block.get("text").and_then(Value::as_str) { final_text.push(text.to_string()); } } "tool_use" => tool_uses.push(block.clone()), _ => {} } } if tool_uses.is_empty() { return Ok(final_text.join("\n")); } // Execute every tool call in this response and collect the results let mut tool_results = Vec::new(); for tool_use in &tool_uses { let name = tool_use .get("name") .and_then(Value::as_str) .context("tool_use block has no name")?; let id = tool_use .get("id") .and_then(Value::as_str) .context("tool_use block has no id")?; let input = tool_use.get("input").cloned().unwrap_or(json!({})); // Add information about the tool call to final text final_text.push(format!("[Calling tool {name} with args {input}]")); // Query the MCP server let mut params = CallToolRequestParams::new(name.to_string()); if let Some(arguments) = input.as_object().cloned() { params = params.with_arguments(arguments); } let tool_result = match session.call_tool(params).await { Ok(result) => result, // A rejected call is the model's mistake to correct, so it // goes back as a failed tool_result rather than ending the // query. Every tool_use still needs a matching result. Err(error) => { final_text.push(format!("[{name} failed: {error}]")); tool_results.push(json!({ "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": id, "content": format!("Tool call {name} failed: {error}"),

title: Build an MCP client
content: {error}"), "is_error": true, })); continue; } }; self.validate_tool_output(name, &tool_result)?; // structured_content is data the application can use directly. if let Some(Value::Array(items)) = &tool_result.structured_content { final_text.push(format!("[{name} returned {} items]", items.len())); } // content is a list of block types; forward only the text ones. let mut payload = tool_result .content .iter() .filter_map(|block| block.as_text().map(|text| text.text.as_str())) .collect::<Vec<_>>() .join("\n"); // A structured result SHOULD also carry serialized JSON in a text // block, but only SHOULD, so fall back to serializing it rather // than sending the model an empty result. if payload.is_empty() { if let Some(structured) = &tool_result.structured_content { payload = structured.to_string(); } } tool_results.push(json!({ "type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": id, "content": payload, "is_error": tool_result.is_error.unwrap_or(false), })); } // Append the assistant's response and all tool results, in one user // message, to the history. Every tool_use needs a matching // tool_result, and the assistant's blocks go back as they arrived. messages.push(Message::assistant(content)); messages.push(Message::user(tool_results)); content = self.request_model(&messages).await?; } // The turn cap was hit. Keep the last response's text. If it asked for // more tools, say they were not run. let mut wants_tools = false; for block in &content { match block_type(block) { "text" => { if let Some(text) = block.get("text").and_then(Value::as_str) { final_text.push(text.to_string()); } } "tool_use" => wants_tools = true, _ => {} } } if wants_tools { final_text.push(format!("[Stopped after {MAX_TOOL_TURNS} tool-use turns]")); } Ok(final_text.join("\n")) } The method sends the user’s query to Claude with the server’s tools and then loops. Each pass collects the text blocks of the reply and gathers its tool_use blocks. When a reply contains no tool use, the collected text is returned.

title: Build an MCP client
content: returned. Otherwise the client calls each requested tool through the MCP session and builds one tool_result block per tool_use. A call the server rejects goes back with is_error set, so Claude can read the message and try something else. A successful result is checked against its output schema. Its text blocks are joined and forwarded to Claude, and when it has no text blocks the serialized structured_content is sent in their place. When structured_content is an array, the client prints the item count as an example of using structured data directly. The assistant’s blocks are appended to the history exactly as they arrived, followed by one user message holding all tool results, and the next request is sent. The loop stops after MAX_TOOL_TURNS rounds. At that point the last reply’s text is kept, and a note is added when Claude asked for more tools.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Add this helper method inside impl MCPClient: /// Call Claude with the current history and return the content blocks of /// its reply, untouched. Tools are passed on every call so Claude can keep /// calling them across turns. async fn request_model(&self, messages: &[Message]) -> Result<Vec<Value>> { let api_key = std::env::var("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY").context("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set")?; // The base URL is configurable so the client can point at a local stand-in. let base_url = std::env::var("ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL").unwrap_or_else(|_| ANTHROPIC_API_BASE.to_string()); let request = MessagesRequest { model: MODEL_ANTHROPIC, max_tokens: MAX_TOKENS, messages, tools: &self.tools, }; let response = self .http .post(format!("{}/v1/messages", base_url.trim_end_matches('/'))) .header("x-api-key", api_key) .header("anthropic-version", ANTHROPIC_VERSION) .json(&request) .send() .await .context("Anthropic request failed")?; let status = response.status(); let body = response .text() .await .context("Unable to read the Anthropic response")?; if !status.is_success() { bail!("Anthropic request failed with {status}: {body}"); } let parsed: MessagesResponse = serde_json::from_str(&body).context("Unable to parse the Anthropic response")?; Ok(parsed.content) } request_model reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on each call and posts the history to /v1/messages with the x-api-key and anthropic-version headers. ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL overrides the endpoint, which allows pointing the client at a local stand-in. Tools are sent on every request so Claude can keep calling them across turns. A non-success status becomes an error that includes the response body. The reply’s content blocks are returned untouched.

title: Build an MCP client
content:
Add the interactive terminal loop inside impl MCPClient: async fn chat_loop(&mut self) -> Result<()> { println!("
MCP Client Started!"); println!("Type your queries or 'quit' to exit."); let mut stdin = BufReader::new(io::stdin()); let mut input = String::new(); loop { print!("
Query: "); std::io::Write::flush(&mut std::io::stdout())?; input.clear(); if stdin.read_line(&mut input).await? == 0 { break; // EOF } let query = input.trim(); if query.eq_ignore_ascii_case("quit") { break; } if query.is_empty() { continue; } match self.process_query(query).await { Ok(response) => println!("
{}", response), Err(err) => println!("
Error: {:#}", err), } } Ok(()) } The loop accepts queries until the user types quit or closes standard input. Query errors are printed without terminating the client. The {:#} format prints the whole anyhow context chain on one line.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Add this method inside impl MCPClient to stop the MCP session and child process. The closing brace ends the impl MCPClient block: async fn cleanup(&mut self) -> Result<()> { if let Some(session) = self.session.take() { let _ = session.cancel().await; } Ok(()) } }

title: Build an MCP client
content: Next, add the asynchronous entry point outside the impl MCPClient block: #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<()> { // .env is optional; the key may come from the environment instead. let _ = dotenvy::dotenv(); let mut args = std::env::args(); let _ = args.next(); let server_args: Vec<String> = args.collect(); if server_args.is_empty() { eprintln!("Usage: cargo run -- <server_script_or_binary> [args...]"); std::process::exit(1); } let mut client = MCPClient::new()?; let result = async { client.connect_to_server(&server_args).await?; // Connecting and listing tools needs no credentials; querying them // does. Matching the Python and TypeScript clients, report and exit // rather than failing, so the connection itself can be exercised // without a key. // Empty counts as unset, as it does in the other clients: `KEY= cmd` // is how the smoke test forces this path. if std::env::var("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY").map_or(true, |key| key.is_empty()) { println!( "\nNo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY found. To query these tools with Claude, set your API key:" ); println!(" export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=your-api-key-here"); return Ok(()); } client.chat_loop().await } .await; let cleanup_result = client.cleanup().await; result?; cleanup_result?; Ok(()) } The entry point loads .env when the file exists, treats all remaining command-line arguments as the server command, connects the client, and ensures cleanup runs before exiting. When ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is unset or empty, the client prints how to set the key and exits after listing the server’s tools. This exercises the MCP connection without credentials.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Finally, add this function outside the impl MCPClient block: fn convert_tools(tools: &[McpTool]) -> Vec<ToolDefinition> { tools .iter() .map(|tool| ToolDefinition { name: tool.name.to_string(), description: tool.description.as_deref().map(str::to_string), input_schema: Value::Object(tool.input_schema.as_ref().clone()), }) .collect() } MCP and the Messages API describe tools with the same information in different Rust types. convert_tools copies each MCP tool’s name, description, and input schema into a ToolDefinition, which serializes to the shape the tools parameter expects. The description is omitted when a tool has none.

title: Build an MCP client
content: Before running the client, confirm the items in src/main.rs are placed at the correct scope: new, validate_tool_output, connect_to_server, process_query, request_model, chat_loop, and cleanup are methods inside the single impl MCPClient block, which opens in Client Initialization and closes after cleanup. user and assistant are methods inside the impl Message block. block_type, main, and convert_tools are functions outside both impl blocks. Rust does not require these items to appear in a particular order, but methods and free functions must be placed in the correct scope. Compare your file with the complete src/main.rs example, then check that it compiles: cargo fmt --check cargo check

title: Client Best Practices
content: Patterns for scaling MCP host applications across many servers and tools. As MCP host applications, such as agents, connect to more MCP servers and accumulate access to hundreds or thousands of tools, naive approaches to tool management break down. Loading every tool definition into the model’s context window upfront wastes tokens, increases latency, and degrades model performance. Passing large intermediate results through the model between sequential tool calls compounds the problem. Two patterns address these challenges: progressive discovery, which controls when tool definitions enter context, and programmatic tool calling, which controls how tools are invoked.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Naive MCP host implementations pass the tool definitions of every connected server directly to the model at the start of each conversation. For a handful of tools, this is perfectly reasonable. But when a host has access to dozens of servers exposing hundreds of tools, those definitions alone can consume the majority of the context window before the model has even read the user’s message. Progressive discovery avoids this: The host fetches tool definitions via tools/list as normal, but defers injecting them into the model’s context. The host provides a lightweight search_tools meta-tool to the model. The host loads full definitions into context only as needed.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Progressive discovery is best used when tool definitions take large parts of the context window. For a small set of tools with tool definitions taking up a small part of the context window, loading all tools is fine. Once the tool definitions take up a significant part of the available context window, clients should switch to progressive discovery. We recommend that clients implement thresholds to determine when to switch: Implement a threshold as a percentage of the context window. For example, 1%-5%. Load tool definitions. Once the threshold is reached, switch to progressive discovery.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Once the model invokes the search_tools tool, we need to choose a search strategy: Keyword-based: Keyword matching (BM25, regex). Simple and effective, particularly for descriptive tool names and descriptions. Embedding-based: Vector-similarity retrieval over tool descriptions. Handles synonyms and semantic matching better. Subagent-based: A secondary model, often a small and fast model such as Claude Haiku or Gemini Flash, selects tools for the task. This usually works very well but can be more costly than embedding-based or keyword-based solutions. Hybrid: Combine approaches. For example, by scoring across keyword and embedding rankings, or choosing different strategies depending on use-case or query. Some model providers already offer built-in tool search. For example, OpenAI and Anthropic support this natively; check your provider’s documentation for an equivalent. When available, you may prefer the platform’s tool search over a custom implementation. Build your own when the provider doesn’t offer one or when you need specialized retrieval logic (e.g., domain-specific ranking or access-control filtering). The three-layer pattern below illustrates a custom search-based approach in detail, but the layered principle (catalog, inspect, execute) applies regardless of retrieval mechanism.

title: Client Best Practices
content: One common implementation for progressive discovery uses a search-based three-layer approach: Layer 1: Catalog. The host exposes a small set of meta-tools for searching available capabilities. A search_tools tool accepts a natural-language query and returns matching tool names with brief descriptions. // The model calls a lightweight search tool search_tools({ query: "update salesforce record" }) // Returns concise matches: names and one-line descriptions only → [ { name: "salesforce_updateRecord", description: "Update fields on a Salesforce object" }, { name: "salesforce_upsertRecord", description: "Insert or update based on external ID" } ] Layer 2: Inspect. Once the model identifies a candidate, it fetches the full definition (input schema, output schema, documentation) for that tool only. // The model inspects only the tool it needs get_tool_details({ name: "salesforce_updateRecord" }); This returns the complete schema for a single tool: { "name": "salesforce_updateRecord", "description": "Updates a record in Salesforce", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "objectType": { "type": "string", "description": "Salesforce object type" }, "recordId": { "type": "string", "description": "Record ID to update" }, "data": { "type": "object", "description": "Fields to update" } }, "required": ["objectType", "recordId", "data"] } } Layer 3: Execute. The model calls the tool with full knowledge of its interface, having loaded only the definitions it needed. This pattern reduces token usage dramatically and can improve tool selection accuracy: the model focuses on a few relevant tools rather than scanning hundreds of irrelevant ones. Other discovery strategies (embeddings, subagents, etc.) follow the same layered principle but substitute different retrieval mechanisms in the catalog layer.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Progressive discovery extends beyond individual tools to entire servers. Rather than connecting to every configured server at startup, a host can: Maintain a registry of available servers and their high-level descriptions. Connect to a server only when the model determines it needs that server’s capabilities. Disconnect servers that are no longer relevant to the current task, freeing context. This works especially well for general-purpose agents, where the user’s intent isn’t known upfront. The agent starts with a minimal set of always-on servers and connects others as needed. Combined with agent skills, a skill file can declare which MCP servers it needs, and the host connects them only when that skill is invoked.

title: Client Best Practices
content: When implementing progressive discovery: Guideline Rationale Offer multiple detail levels Let the model choose between name-only, name-and-description, or full-schema responses. Cache tool definitions Once fetched from a server, memoize the definition host-side so re-injecting it later doesn’t need another tools/list round trip. This is separate from what’s currently in the model’s context. Refresh on list_changed Re-index the search catalog when a server sends notifications/tools/list_changed. Group tools by server Present tools organized by their source server so the model can reason about related capabilities.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Each list result (such as tools/list), as well as each server/discover and resources/read result, carries ttlMs and cacheScope hints. Follow them as defined in the specification’s caching utility. In particular, treat a cached list as stale once a list_changed notification arrives, even before its TTL expires.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Most providers cache the prompt prefix, including the tools array. Adding or removing tool definitions mid-conversation invalidates that cache, and the resulting miss can cost more tokens than the definitions you removed. To preserve caching: Append newly discovered definitions after the cache breakpoint rather than re-sorting the tools array, or route every call through a single stable call_tool({name, args}) meta-tool so the array never changes. Treat server disconnection as a conversation-boundary operation rather than a per-turn one. Consult your provider’s caching documentation alongside the tool-search links above.

title: Client Best Practices
content: With direct tool calling, every tool invocation is a round trip: the model generates a tool call, the client executes it, and the full result flows back into the model’s context. When a task requires chaining multiple tools (read a document, transform it, write it somewhere else), each intermediate result passes through the model, consuming tokens and adding latency even when it has nothing to do with them. Programmatic tool calling (sometimes called “code mode”) provides a way for clients to compose tool calls effectively. Instead of calling tools directly, the model writes code that calls tools. The code executes in a sandboxed environment, and only the final result returns to the model. Programmatic tool calling is powerful and allows for more efficient use of MCP tools and resources, but requires clients to implement a sandbox environment.

title: Client Best Practices
content: The host converts MCP tool schemas into a typed API available inside a sandbox. When the model needs tools, it writes a script and executes it. Step 1: Generate a programmatic API from MCP schemas. The host reads each server’s tool definitions and produces typed functions based on each tool’s arguments and outputSchema: // Auto-generated from the Logging MCP server's tool schema interface LogEntry { timestamp: string; message: string; level: string; } function logging_getLogs(input: { level: "error" | "warn" | "info"; since: number; }): Promise<{ entries: LogEntry[] }> { return mcp.callTool<{ entries: LogEntry[] }>("logging_getLogs", input); } // Auto-generated from the Ticketing MCP server's tool schema function ticketing_createIssue(input: { title: string; body?: string; priority: "low" | "medium" | "high"; }): Promise<{ issueId: string }> { return mcp.callTool<{ issueId: string }>("ticketing_createIssue", input); } MCP Servers can provide an optional outputSchema for each tool. When an output schema is present, the host can produce precise return types (like LogEntry above). When an output schema is absent, prefer the simple path: Use a generic type and move on. Accept any or string and handle the unstructured output downstream. The real fix is for server authors to provide outputSchema. Extract a typed result using a fast model, for single-shot calls outside loops. Expose a host-brokered extract(value, ExpectedType) helper through the same stub-interception path as MCP tool calls so the sandbox itself never opens a network connection. The helper routes to a small model (for example, Claude Haiku or Gemini Flash) to coerce the value into ExpectedType. This adds per-call latency and can hallucinate or drop fields, so validate the result against ExpectedType before use. Step 2: The model writes code against these APIs. Rather than making separate tool calls with full results flowing through context between them, the model writes a single script. Consider a task

title: Client Best Practices
content: task like “find all error logs from the past hour and file a ticket for each unique error.” With direct tool calling, thousands of log entries would flow through the model’s context. With code, the model filters in the sandbox: // Model-generated code, executes in sandbox const logs = await logging_getLogs({ level: "error", since: Date.now() - 3600000, }); // Filter and deduplicate inside the sandbox, not in the model's context const uniqueErrors = new Map<string, LogEntry>(); for (const log of logs.entries) { if (!uniqueErrors.has(log.message)) { uniqueErrors.set(log.message, log); } } for (const [message, log] of uniqueErrors) { await ticketing_createIssue({ title: `Error: ${message}`, body: `First seen: ${log.timestamp}\nOccurrences: ${ logs.entries.filter((l) => l.message === message).length }`, priority: "high", }); } console.log( `Filed ${uniqueErrors.size} tickets from ${logs.entries.length} error logs`, ); Step 3: The sandbox executes the code. Function calls inside the sandbox are intercepted and routed back to the appropriate MCP server through the host broker. The log data and ticket creation flow directly between servers without ever entering the model’s context. Only the console.log output, a single summary line, returns to the model.

title: Client Best Practices
content: The right sandbox depends on the language you want the model to write, your host application’s language, and how much isolation you need. The table lists example runtimes rather than endorsements; evaluate maturity for your use case: Sandboxed language Runtime / Library Host language Approach JavaScript Deno, isolated-vm Rust / Node / CLI V8-based runtimes with fine-grained permissions. Can disable all permissions for full lockdown. Python Monty (experimental) Rust Minimal Python interpreter built for AI use cases. No I/O by default. TypeScript pctx (early-stage) Python / Rust Incorporates code mode concepts as a library, with low-level Rust support. Any (via Wasm) Wasmtime Rust / C / Go Compile any language to Wasm and run it with capability-based security. Regardless of sandbox, the integration pattern is the same: the host injects function stubs, intercepts calls over an in-process or stdio channel (so network permissions can stay fully denied), and dispatches them as tools/call requests to MCP servers.

title: Client Best Practices
content: The implementation has three components: The sandbox runs model-generated code in an isolated environment with no direct network access. Its only interface to the outside world is through the generated function stubs, which route calls back to the host. The host acts as a broker. It receives function calls from the sandbox, maps them to the correct MCP server, executes the tool call, and returns the result to the sandbox. Authorization tokens and credentials are held by the host and never exposed to the generated code. The model sees only what the sandbox returns, typically the output of console.log statements or a final return value. This gives the model (and the client developer) precise control over what enters the context window.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Programmatic tool calling introduces a code execution surface that requires careful sandboxing: Per-call authorization: The broker is still the MCP host for spec purposes. Apply the same human-in-the-loop confirmation policy to sandbox-originated calls that you apply to direct calls (see Tools: Security). Approving the script does not grant blanket approval for every tool call it makes at runtime; hosts may grant categorical approval (for example, “allow ticketing_createIssue for this script run”) rather than prompting per iteration, but the broker must still evaluate each call against that grant. Cross-server data flow: Tool results from one server are untrusted input to another. The broker should apply the same input-review policy to brokered calls as to direct ones; output truncation alone does not prevent exfiltration. Network isolation: The sandbox should have no direct network access. All external communication flows through the host broker, which enforces authorization and access control. No credential exposure: API keys and tokens are held by the host. The generated code calls typed functions; the host adds authentication when forwarding to servers. Resource limits: Set timeouts and memory limits on sandbox execution to prevent runaway scripts. Output filtering: Validate and truncate sandbox console output before feeding it back to the model.

title: Client Best Practices
content: MCP tool errors arrive as a successful response with isError: true rather than a transport failure. Generated wrappers should convert this into a thrown exception so model-authored code can use try/catch. If an uncaught error terminates the script, surface it as the script’s result so the model can self-correct; the model is responsible for reporting any partial side effects already committed.

title: Client Best Practices
content: Progressive discovery and programmatic tool calling work well together. The model uses discovery tools to identify which tools it needs, loads their schemas, and then writes a single script that calls multiple tools in one execution pass. This combination minimizes both the token cost of tool definitions and the token cost of tool results, keeping the model’s context focused on reasoning rather than passing data through it.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: Learn how to implement secure authorization for MCP servers using OAuth 2.1 to protect sensitive resources and operations Authorization in the Model Context Protocol (MCP) secures access to sensitive resources and operations exposed by MCP servers. If your MCP server handles user data or administrative actions, authorization lets only permitted users reach its endpoints. MCP authorization follows OAuth 2.1 and works with any authorization or identity system that meets its requirements. This guide explains the flow, then shows how to protect a small server. The full requirements are in the Authorization specification.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: Authorization is optional for MCP servers. It is strongly recommended when: Your server works with user-specific data such as emails, documents, or databases You need to audit who performed which actions Your server grants access to its APIs that require user consent You’re building for enterprise environments with strict access controls You want to rate-limit or track usage per user Authorization for Local MCP ServersThe OAuth flow in this guide is for HTTP-based transports. Servers that use the stdio transport should retrieve credentials from the environment instead. They run locally, so they can also use credentials from libraries embedded in the server.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
header: The Authorization Flow: Step by Step
content: Three parties take part. Your MCP server is an OAuth resource server. In this role it validates access tokens and doesn’t issue them. The MCP client is an OAuth client acting on behalf of a user. The authorization server authenticates the user and issues tokens for your MCP server. It can be a separate service or be hosted together with the MCP server. 1 Initial Request When a client sends a request without a valid token, your server responds with 401 Unauthorized. The WWW-Authenticate header can point to the Protected Resource Metadata (PRM) document. It should also name the scopes needed to access the resource. HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized WWW-Authenticate: Bearer resource_metadata="https://your-server.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp", scope="mcp:tools" The client should request the scopes named in the challenge. If the challenge names none, it should request everything in the PRM document’s scopes_supported. If that is missing too, it leaves out the scope parameter. See Scope Selection Strategy.A server must include the resource_metadata pointer or serve the PRM document at a well-known URI. It can do both. When the pointer is missing, the client first tries /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource followed by the path of the MCP endpoint. It then tries the same URL without the path. See Protected Resource Metadata Discovery Requirements. 2 Protected Resource Metadata Discovery The client fetches the PRM document to learn which authorization servers the MCP server trusts. authorization_servers must contain at least one entry. { "resource": "https://your-server.com/mcp", "authorization_servers": ["https://auth.your-server.com"], "scopes_supported": ["mcp:tools"] } resource identifies your MCP server. Use the exact URL that clients connect to. RFC 9728 Section 3.3 says clients must not use a document whose resource doesn’t match. 3 Authorization Server Discovery The client picks an authorization server and fetches its metadata. The metadata can be at an

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
header: The Authorization Flow: Step by Step
content: an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata or an OpenID Connect Discovery URL. Clients must support both and try the URLs in the order the specification defines. { "issuer": "https://auth.your-server.com", "authorization_endpoint": "https://auth.your-server.com/authorize", "token_endpoint": "https://auth.your-server.com/token", "jwks_uri": "https://auth.your-server.com/jwks", "response_types_supported": ["code"], "grant_types_supported": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported": ["none"], "code_challenge_methods_supported": ["S256"], "client_id_metadata_document_supported": true, "authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported": true } The client must check two of these values: issuer must be identical to the issuer identifier used to build the metadata URL. If it isn’t, the client must not use the document. code_challenge_methods_supported must be present. If it’s absent, the client must refuse to proceed, because the authorization server doesn’t support PKCE. 4 Client Registration The client needs a client ID that the authorization server accepts. The options are summarized in Client Registration Approaches. 5 User Authorization The client opens a browser at the authorization_endpoint. The request includes a PKCE code_challenge and the resource parameter (RFC 8707), set to the MCP server’s URL: GET /authorize?response_type=code &client_id=https%3A%2F%2Fapp.example.com%2Foauth%2Fclient-metadata.json &redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2F127.0.0.1%3A8090%2Fcallback &scope=mcp%3Atools &resource=https%3A%2F%2Fyour-server.com%2Fmcp &code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM &code_challenge_method=S256 &state=af0ifjsldkj HTTP/1.1 Host: auth.your-server.com The line breaks in this example are only there to make it easier to read.After the user logs in and consents, the authorization server redirects back to the client with a code and the state. If it supports RFC 9207, it also returns iss.Before it opens the browser, the

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
header: The Authorization Flow: Step by Step
content: the client must record the issuer from the validated metadata. Before it exchanges the code, it must validate iss against that issuer, without normalizing either value. If the authorization server advertises support for iss, the client must reject a response that leaves it out. The same check applies to error responses. If it fails, the client must not act on the error or display it.The client should also discard a response whose state is missing or different from the value it sent.The client then sends the code, the PKCE verifier, and the same resource value to the token_endpoint. It receives an access token, and the authorization server can choose to return a refresh token too: { "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs...", "token_type": "Bearer", "expires_in": 3600, "scope": "mcp:tools" } 6 Making Authenticated Requests The client sends the access token in the Authorization header of every HTTP request, and never in the URL: POST /mcp HTTP/1.1 Host: your-server.com Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIs... Content-Type: application/json Accept: application/json, text/event-stream MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28 Mcp-Method: tools/list { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/list", "params": { "_meta": { "io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion": "2026-07-28", "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo": { "name": "ExampleClient", "version": "1.0.0" }, "io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities": {} } } } Before it processes the request, the MCP server validates the token and checks that the token was issued for this server. An invalid or expired token gets a 401.If the token is valid but lacks a scope, the server should respond with 403 Forbidden and an insufficient_scope challenge: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_scope", scope="mcp:tools", resource_metadata="https://your-server.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp" The client should then start a step-up authorization flow. It requests the scopes in the challenge

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
header: The Authorization Flow: Step by Step
content: challenge together with the scopes it requested before, and it should limit how often it retries.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: Approach When to Use Pre-registration The client already has credentials for this authorization server Client ID Metadata Documents Client and server have no prior relationship (most common) A client that supports both should try them in that order. If neither is available, it should ask the user to enter the client ID, and the client secret if there is one, of a client registered with the authorization server. See Client Registration. Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) is deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28. New implementations should use Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) instead.Existing clients can fall back to DCR before asking the user for a client ID and secret. This is applicable if the authorization server doesn’t support CIMD and allows clients to register at runtime through its registration_endpoint.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: With a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), the client uses an HTTPS URL as its client_id and hosts a JSON document there. The authorization server fetches the document and validates it when it receives an authorization request. { "client_id": "https://app.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json", "client_name": "Example MCP Client", "redirect_uris": ["http://127.0.0.1:8090/callback"], "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "response_types": ["code"], "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none" } The URL must use https and contain a path, such as /oauth/client-metadata.json. The document must contain at least client_id, client_name, and redirect_uris, and its client_id must match the URL exactly. Authorization servers advertise support with "client_id_metadata_document_supported": true. A client can use the same client ID with every authorization server that supports CIMD. It doesn’t need to register again if your MCP server changes authorization servers.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: The client ID is set up in advance, along with credentials if they’re needed. They can be built into the client or entered by the user. Credentials belong to the authorization server that issued them. Clients must store them by issuer and never use them with another one. See Authorization Server Binding.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: Use an existing identity provider or authorization server product. Client registration happens between the client and the authorization server, so your MCP server needs no registration code. Check these points before you choose one: Audience. Your MCP server must reject tokens that weren’t issued for it. The resource value from the client should become the token’s audience, which is the aud claim in a JWT. Some products need a setting for this, or let you configure the audience on a scope instead. Others always use their own identifier. In that case, compare the audience with that identifier, and keep your server’s URL as the PRM resource. The identifier must belong to this MCP server only, so don’t share one application registration between servers. Metadata. It must serve metadata through RFC 8414 or OpenID Connect Discovery. The metadata must contain code_challenge_methods_supported. Look at the real document, because some products support PKCE but leave this value out, and clients that follow the specification then refuse to connect. CIMD. It should support CIMD, which it advertises with client_id_metadata_document_supported. In some products you have to enable this, or list the client domains you accept. Token format. The examples below need signed JWT access tokens. Otherwise, you need an introspection endpoint. Public clients. Many MCP clients have no secret. The authorization server must accept them, and its token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported should contain none. Scopes. Define a scope such as mcp:tools and make it available to the clients that will connect. Some products add a prefix to scope names. If yours does, use the full name everywhere the examples use mcp:tools. If you define more than one scope, read Scope Minimization, and list only the scopes needed for basic use in scopes_supported. Token lifetime. Access tokens should be short-lived, because a stolen token works until it expires. The authorization server must rotate refresh tokens for public

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: public clients. Issuer in responses. It should return iss in authorization responses. If it does, it must advertise authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported. Testing LocallyYou can run an authorization server on your own machine. For example, Keycloak has experimental support for CIMD and resource indicators. To enable both, start it with --features=cimd,resource-indicators. You then have to create a client policy for CIMD and add your server’s URL to its resource indicator allow list.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: The examples below protect an MCP server that has one tool, add. Each server runs at http://localhost:3000/mcp, requires the mcp:tools scope, and accepts JWT access tokens signed with RS256. Before you run one, change these values: ISSUER is the exact issuer value from your authorization server’s metadata. METADATA_URL is the URL of that metadata. If the issuer has a path, as in https://auth.example.com/tenant1, the RFC 8414 URL is https://auth.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/tenant1, and the OpenID Connect URL is usually https://auth.example.com/tenant1/.well-known/openid-configuration. RS256 (RsaSha256 in C#) is the signing algorithm. Change it if your authorization server uses a different one. In Python, the published keys must then have an alg value. mcp:tools is the required scope. The expected audience is the server URL. Change it if your authorization server puts its own identifier in aud. It is the audience option in TypeScript and Python, and ValidAudience in C#. In the C# example, the first two are called issuer and metadataUrl. The TypeScript and Python examples fetch the metadata at startup, so they exit if the authorization server can’t be reached. TypeScript Python C# Install the TypeScript SDK packages, a JWT library, and Zod 4: npm install @modelcontextprotocol/server@^2.3.0 @modelcontextprotocol/express@^2.0.2 \ @modelcontextprotocol/node express jose zod@4 npm install --save-dev tsx @types/express Set "type": "module" in package.json, and create server.ts: import { createMcpExpressApp, getOAuthProtectedResourceMetadataUrl, mcpAuthMetadataRouter, requireBearerAuth, } from "@modelcontextprotocol/express"; import { toNodeHandler } from "@modelcontextprotocol/node"; import { createMcpHandler, McpServer, OAuthError, OAuthErrorCode, } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server"; import type { AuthInfo, OAuthMetadata } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server"; import { createRemoteJWKSet, errors, jwtVerify } from "jose"; import * as z from "zod"; //

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: // The authorization server's issuer identifier, and where it publishes metadata const ISSUER = "https://auth.example.com"; const METADATA_URL = "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server"; // The URL clients connect to, which is also the audience of their tokens const MCP_SERVER_URL = new URL("http://localhost:3000/mcp"); const metadataResponse = await fetch(METADATA_URL); if (!metadataResponse.ok) { throw new Error(`Metadata request failed: ${metadataResponse.status}`); } const oauthMetadata = (await metadataResponse.json()) as OAuthMetadata; if (oauthMetadata.issuer !== ISSUER) { throw new Error(`Unexpected issuer: ${oauthMetadata.issuer}`); } const jwks = createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(String(oauthMetadata.jwks_uri))); // Errors that mean the keys could not be fetched, not that the token is bad const JWKS_OUTAGE = [ "ERR_JWKS_TIMEOUT", "ERR_JWKS_INVALID", "ERR_JOSE_GENERIC", ]; async function verifyAccessToken(token: string): Promise<AuthInfo> { try { const { payload } = await jwtVerify(token, jwks, { algorithms: ["RS256"], issuer: ISSUER, audience: MCP_SERVER_URL.href, requiredClaims: ["exp"], clockTolerance: 30, }); return { token, clientId: String(payload.client_id ?? payload.azp ?? ""), scopes: typeof payload.scope === "string" ? payload.scope.split(" ") : [], expiresAt: payload.exp, // jwtVerify has checked that the token's audience is this server resource: MCP_SERVER_URL, extra: { sub: payload.sub }, }; } catch (error) { // requireBearerAuth answers 401 for an OAuthError with this code, and 500 // for any other exception. if ( error instanceof errors.JOSEError && !JWKS_OUTAGE.includes(error.code) ) { throw new OAuthError(OAuthErrorCode.InvalidToken, "Invalid access token"); } console.error("Could not verify the token:", error); throw error; } } function createServer() { const server = new McpServer({ name: "math", version: "1.0.0" }); server.registerTool( "add", { description: "Add two numbers together", inputSchema: z.object({ a:

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: a: z.number(), b: z.number() }), }, async ({ a, b }) => ({ content: [{ type: "text", text: String(a + b) }], }), ); return server; } const app = createMcpExpressApp(); app.use( mcpAuthMetadataRouter({ oauthMetadata, resourceServerUrl: MCP_SERVER_URL, scopesSupported: ["mcp:tools"], }), ); const requireAuth = requireBearerAuth({ verifier: { verifyAccessToken }, requiredScopes: ["mcp:tools"], expectedResource: MCP_SERVER_URL, resourceMetadataUrl: getOAuthProtectedResourceMetadataUrl(MCP_SERVER_URL), }); const handler = toNodeHandler(createMcpHandler(createServer)); app.all("/mcp", requireAuth, (req, res) => void handler(req, res, req.body)); app.listen(3000, "127.0.0.1", (error) => { if (error) throw error; console.log(`MCP server listening on ${MCP_SERVER_URL}`); }); mcpAuthMetadataRouter serves the PRM document at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp. It also mirrors the authorization server metadata for older clients that look for it on the MCP server. requireBearerAuth runs your verifier on every request. It answers a missing or invalid token with a 401 challenge, and a missing scope with a 403 challenge. jwtVerify checks the signature, issuer, audience, and lifetime. Keep its audience option, because expectedResource doesn’t look at the token. expectedResource refuses a token if the verifier reports a different resource or none. It requires @modelcontextprotocol/express 2.0.2, and earlier versions ignore it. createMcpExpressApp validates the Host and Origin headers of a server bound to localhost. Run the server: npx tsx server.ts To require a scope for a single tool, see Require authorization in the TypeScript SDK documentation. Install the Python SDK, HTTPX2, and PyJWT with the crypto extra that RS256 needs: pip install "mcp>=2.2" "httpx2>=2.5" "pyjwt[crypto]>=2.14" Create server.py: import asyncio import httpx2 import jwt from mcp.server import MCPServer from mcp.server.auth.provider import AccessToken, TokenVerifier from mcp.server.auth.settings import

Returning None from verify_token produces a 401 challenge. A token without one of required_scopes gets a 403 challenge. jwt.decode checks the signature, issuer, audience, and lifetime. Keep its audience argument, because validate_token_resource doesn’t look at the token. It makes the SDK refuse a token if AccessToken.resource isn’t resource_server_url. It requires version 2.2, and earlier versions ignore it. The SDK doesn’t put scope in its challenges. After a 401, clients find the scopes in scopes_supported instead. After a 403, some clients request only the scopes they already have, so step-up authorization might not get the missing scope. AddJwtBearer downloads the signing keys and validates the signature, issuer, audience, and lifetime. By default it accepts tokens for five minutes after they expire, so the example sets ClockSkew. The example sets MetadataAddress because the Authority option only looks for OpenID Connect Discovery metadata. The mcp:tools policy enforces the scope. RequireAuthorization() on its own accepts any valid token. OnChallenge and OnForbidden write the 401 and 403

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: 403 challenges. The SDK’s own 401 challenge has no scope, and behind a proxy its resource_metadata URL can be wrong. It sends no 403 challenge. JWT bearer authentication only downloads metadata over HTTPS. With any other URL, requests fail with a 500. If your local authorization server uses plain HTTP, set options.RequireHttpsMetadata = false in AddJwtBearer. Do this only in development. OnAuthenticationFailed makes the server answer 500 if it has never been able to download the signing keys. Without it, ASP.NET Core answers 401. ASP.NET Core downloads the signing keys again every 12 hours, or when it sees an unknown key. It answers 401 for an unknown key until the download is done. By default it does this at most once every five minutes, so a new key can be refused for that long. The example sets RefreshInterval to shorten this. The transport specification requires servers to validate the Origin header. The SDK doesn’t do this, so the example does it in middleware. Run the server: dotnet run For per-tool authorization with [Authorize], see Identity and Role Propagation in the C# SDK documentation. A failed [Authorize] check on a tool returns a JSON-RPC error and no 403 challenge, so clients can’t start step-up authorization from it.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: If your authorization server issues opaque tokens, use its token introspection endpoint instead of validating a JWT. Its URL is the introspection_endpoint value in the metadata. The endpoint requires authorization, so your MCP server needs its own credentials at the authorization server. If you use HTTP Basic authentication, form-encode the client ID and secret first. The credentials must be allowed to introspect tokens for this server. If they aren’t, the response for a valid token has active set to false. If active is false, reject the token. If it is true, check that aud contains the expected audience before you report the resource to the SDK. Check scope and exp too. These values are optional in the RFC, so make sure your authorization server returns them, and reject a token whose aud is missing. If the endpoint can’t be reached or returns an error status, even a 401, treat that as an outage. If you cache tokens or results, encrypt the tokens and delete each entry no later than the token expires. Keep your server’s credentials in a secret manager. In TypeScript and Python, make the call in the verifier. In C#, replace AddJwtBearer with an authentication handler that supports introspection.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: Change the server URL to the exact https URL that clients connect to. It is used as the PRM resource and as the expected audience. If its path isn’t /mcp, change the route too. It is the app.all path in TypeScript and the streamable_http_path argument of mcp.run in Python. The C# example takes it from the URL. In TypeScript, new URL() adds a trailing slash to a URL that has no path, and the token’s aud then has to include it. Clients must reach your server over HTTPS. The examples serve plain HTTP, so put them behind a reverse proxy or load balancer that terminates TLS and keeps the original Host header. If it runs on the same machine, keep listening on localhost and change only the accepted hosts and origins. The examples listen only on localhost and reject requests with any other Host header. Configure the hosts and browser origins you accept: TypeScript: Pass host, allowedHosts, and allowedOrigins to createMcpExpressApp, and change the address given to app.listen. Both lists take host names without a scheme or port. If no browser client connects, pass an empty allowedOrigins list, because the SDK doesn’t check Origin without it. Set NODE_ENV=production so that Express doesn’t send stack traces to clients. Python: Pass host and a TransportSecuritySettings object as transport_security to mcp.run. Import the class from mcp.server.transport_security, and set its allowed_hosts and allowed_origins. The SDK checks neither header if you change host and leave this out. A host must match the Host header exactly, including the port if it has one, and an origin must include its scheme. End an entry with :* to accept any port. C#: Change the URL given to app.Run to the address to listen on, such as http://0.0.0.0:3000. Change allowedOrigins, whose entries include the scheme, and allowedHosts, whose entries have no scheme or port. Accepting an origin doesn’t enable CORS. Clients that run in a browser also need CORS middleware that answers preflight requests before

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: before authentication and exposes the WWW-Authenticate header. This protocol revision has no sessions, so ignore the Mcp-Session-Id header if your server supports only this revision. If it also accepts older clients, never use a session ID as proof of who the caller is. See Session Hijacking in the 2025-11-25 documentation.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: First check discovery. These requests don’t need a token: curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/mcp curl http://localhost:3000/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp The first command should print a 401 with a WWW-Authenticate header. The second should print the PRM document, which contains your server’s URL and your issuer. Also open your METADATA_URL and check that it contains code_challenge_methods_supported. Some clients work without it and others refuse to connect. Then run the full flow with the MCP Inspector, which needs Node.js 22.23.4+, 24.22.1+, or 26.12.1+. The command below runs the login flow and calls the tool: npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector --cli http://localhost:3000/mcp --transport http \ --protocol-era modern \ --client-metadata-url https://app.example.com/oauth/client-metadata.json \ --method tools/call --tool-name add --tool-arg a=2 b=3 --protocol-era modern makes the Inspector use the 2026-07-28 protocol. By default, the Inspector’s redirect URI is http://127.0.0.1:6276/oauth/callback (change it with --callback-url; it must be a loopback address). --client-metadata-url is the URL of a metadata document that you host, with this redirect URI in its redirect_uris. The authorization server must be able to fetch it. For a pre-registered client, register the redirect URI and use --client-id instead, with --client-secret if the client has a secret. You can also connect from a client such as Visual Studio Code. Run MCP: Add Server from the Command Palette, choose HTTP, and enter http://localhost:3000/mcp. Common Issues The authorization server rejects the client ID. It must be able to fetch the client_id URL from its own network. If it has a list of trusted client domains, the list must include the URL’s host. The metadata document is invalid. Its client_id must be identical to its URL, including any trailing slash. The redirect URI in the request must be in redirect_uris. Authorization servers should accept any port for a loopback IP address,

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: address, but some compare the port too. The authorization server rejects the resource value. Register your server’s URL exactly as clients send it, including the path and any trailing slash. The error might be invalid_target. The Inspector prints auth_required after a successful login. Your server refused the new token. The command prints the same message for a 401 and a 403. To see which one it is, send the token with curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/mcp -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>". The Inspector still fails after you fix the configuration. It keeps tokens and client details between runs. Add --relogin to discard them. Every token gets a 401. Decode a test token. iss must be exactly the same as ISSUER, and aud must contain exactly the expected audience, http://localhost:3000/mcp in the examples. If the token isn’t a JWT, see Opaque Tokens. Check too that the clocks of the two servers agree. Every token gets a 403. If the response has an insufficient_scope error, the token’s scope claim doesn’t contain mcp:tools. Some authorization servers use a claim such as scp, or an array instead of a string. Change the code that reads the claim. If the token uses a shorter name than clients request, convert it to the full name there. If there is no such error, the Host or Origin header might have been refused. For a refused Host, the Python SDK answers 421 and ASP.NET Core answers 400. The client refuses to start the flow. Check that the authorization server metadata has code_challenge_methods_supported and that its issuer matches the PRM document.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
header: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
content: Read Security Best Practices for attacks and how to prevent them, and Security Considerations for the requirements in the specification. These topics matter most in the following cases: Your server calls other APIs: It must get a separate token for each of them. See Token Passthrough. Your server proxies OAuth with one static client ID: It must get the user’s consent for each MCP client. See Confused Deputy Problem. Your tools return state handles: See State Handle Hijacking. You build a client: See Mix-Up Attacks, OAuth Authorization URL Validation, and Server-Side Request Forgery. The list below covers other common mistakes in a protected server and its authorization server: Don’t write your own token validation. Use well-tested libraries for signature checks, claims validation, and authorization decisions. Always validate the audience. A correctly signed token from your authorization server might be meant for another service. Compare the audience exactly with your server’s URL, or with the identifier your authorization server uses for this server only. Don’t accept a value that several servers share, such as api. Accept only access tokens. Never accept an ID token. If your authorization server follows RFC 9068, check that the token’s typ header is at+jwt or application/at+jwt. The examples don’t check it, because many authorization servers use another value. Accept only one issuer. Reject tokens from other issuers or tenants, unless your server is meant to be multi-tenant. Return complete challenges. Where your SDK allows it, include resource_metadata and scope in 401 and 403 challenges. List every scope the operation needs at once. Leave offline_access out of challenges and scopes_supported, because your server doesn’t need refresh tokens. Return 5xx during an outage. If your server can’t reach the JWKS or introspection endpoint, return a 5xx status, as the TypeScript and Python examples do. The C# example does this only until it has downloaded the keys once. A

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
header: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
content: A 401 makes users log in again, and that doesn’t fix the problem. Separate client and server credentials. Don’t use your MCP server’s introspection credentials in end-user flows. Don’t log credentials. Remove Authorization headers, tokens, authorization codes, and secrets from your logs. Return generic errors to clients and keep the details in your own logs. Restrict Dynamic Client Registration. If your authorization server supports DCR with an open registration_endpoint, anyone can register a client. Disable DCR if your clients don’t depend on it. Otherwise, restrict registration with controls such as trusted hosts and rate limits.

title: Understanding Authorization in MCP
content: MCP authorization builds on these specifications: OAuth 2.1: The core authorization framework RFC 9728: Protected Resource Metadata RFC 8414: Authorization Server Metadata OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0: The alternative to RFC 8414 RFC 8707: Resource Indicators RFC 9207: Authorization Server Issuer Identification OAuth Client ID Metadata Document: Client IDs that are URLs RFC 6750: Bearer Token Usage For more details, see: Authorization Specification Security Best Practices Authorization Extensions, for machine-to-machine and enterprise-managed authorization Available MCP SDKs

title: Security Best Practices
content: Security considerations, attack vectors, and best practices for MCP implementations

title: Security Best Practices
content: This document provides security considerations for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), complementing the MCP Authorization specification. This document identifies security risks, attack vectors, and best practices specific to MCP implementations. The primary audience for this document includes developers implementing MCP authorization flows, MCP server operators, and security professionals evaluating MCP-based systems. This document should be read alongside the MCP Authorization specification and OAuth 2.0 security best practices.

title: Security Best Practices
content: This section gives a detailed description of attacks on MCP implementations, along with potential countermeasures.

title: Security Best Practices
content: Attackers can exploit MCP proxy servers that connect to third-party APIs, creating “confused deputy” vulnerabilities. This attack allows malicious clients to obtain authorization codes without proper user consent by exploiting the combination of static client IDs, dynamic client registration, and consent cookies. Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28. The attack still applies to MCP proxy servers that support it. Terminology MCP Proxy Server : An MCP server that connects MCP clients to third-party APIs, offering MCP features while delegating operations and acting as a single OAuth client to the third-party API server. Third-Party Authorization Server : Authorization server that protects the third-party API. It may lack dynamic client registration support, requiring the MCP proxy to use a static client ID for all requests. Third-Party API : The protected resource server that provides the actual API functionality. Access to this API requires tokens issued by the third-party authorization server. Static Client ID : A fixed OAuth 2.0 client identifier used by the MCP proxy server when communicating with the third-party authorization server. This Client ID refers to the MCP server acting as a client to the Third-Party API. It is the same value for all MCP server to Third-Party API interactions regardless of which MCP client initiated the request. Vulnerable Conditions This attack becomes possible when all of the following conditions are present: MCP proxy server uses a static client ID with a third-party authorization server MCP proxy server allows MCP clients to dynamically register (each getting their own client_id) The third-party authorization server sets a consent cookie after the first authorization MCP proxy server does not implement proper per-client consent before forwarding to third-party authorization Architecture and Attack Flows Normal OAuth proxy usage (preserves user consent) Malicious OAuth proxy usage (skips user

title: Security Best Practices
content: user consent) Attack Description When an MCP proxy server uses a static client ID to authenticate with a third-party authorization server, the following attack becomes possible: A user authenticates normally through the MCP proxy server to access the third-party API During this flow, the third-party authorization server sets a cookie on the user agent indicating consent for the static client ID An attacker later sends the user a malicious link containing a crafted authorization request which contains a malicious redirect URI along with a new dynamically registered client ID When the user clicks the link, their browser still has the consent cookie from the previous legitimate request The third-party authorization server detects the cookie and skips the consent screen The MCP authorization code is redirected to the attacker’s server (specified in the malicious redirect_uri parameter during dynamic client registration) The attacker exchanges the stolen authorization code for access tokens for the MCP server without the user’s explicit approval The attacker now has access to the third-party API as the compromised user Mitigation To prevent confused deputy attacks, MCP proxy servers MUST implement per-client consent and proper security controls as detailed below. Consent Flow Implementation The following diagram shows how to properly implement per-client consent that runs before the third-party authorization flow: Required Protections Per-Client Consent Storage MCP proxy servers MUST: Maintain a registry of approved client_id values per user Check this registry before initiating the third-party authorization flow Store consent decisions securely (server-side database, or server specific cookies) Consent UI Requirements The MCP-level consent page MUST: Clearly identify the requesting MCP client by name Display the specific third-party API scopes being requested Show the registered redirect_uri where tokens will be sent Implement CSRF protection (e.g., state parameter,

title: Security Best Practices
content: parameter, CSRF tokens) Prevent iframing via frame-ancestors CSP directive or X-Frame-Options: DENY to prevent clickjacking Consent Cookie Security If using cookies to track consent decisions, they MUST: Use __Host- prefix for cookie names Set Secure, HttpOnly, and SameSite=Lax attributes Be cryptographically signed or use server-side sessions Bind to the specific client_id (not just “user has consented”) Redirect URI Validation The MCP proxy server MUST: Validate that the redirect_uri in authorization requests exactly matches the registered URI Reject requests if the redirect_uri has changed without re-registration Use exact string matching (not pattern matching or wildcards) OAuth State Parameter Validation The OAuth state parameter is critical to prevent authorization code interception and CSRF attacks. Proper state validation ensures that consent approval at the authorization endpoint is enforced at the callback endpoint. MCP proxy servers implementing OAuth flows MUST: Generate a cryptographically secure random state value for each authorization request Store the state value server-side (in a secure session store or encrypted cookie) only after consent has been explicitly approved Set the state tracking cookie/session immediately before redirecting to the third-party identity provider (not before consent approval) Validate at the callback endpoint that the state query parameter exactly matches the stored value in the callback request’s cookies or in the request’s cookie-based session Reject any callback requests where the state parameter is missing or does not match Ensure state values are single-use (delete after validation) and have a short expiration time (e.g., 10 minutes) The consent cookie or session containing the state value MUST NOT be set until after the user has approved the consent screen at the MCP server’s authorization endpoint. Setting this cookie before consent approval renders the consent screen ineffective, as an attacker could bypass it by

title: Security Best Practices
content: by crafting a malicious authorization request.

title: Security Best Practices
content: “Token passthrough” is an anti-pattern where an MCP server accepts tokens from an MCP client without validating that the tokens were properly issued to the MCP server and passes them through to the downstream API. An attacker can gain unauthorized access or otherwise compromise an MCP server if the server accepts tokens issued for other resources. This vulnerability has two critical dimensions: Audience validation failures. When an MCP server doesn’t verify that tokens were specifically intended for it (for example, via the audience claim, as mentioned in RFC9068), it may accept tokens originally issued for other services. This breaks a fundamental OAuth security boundary, allowing attackers to reuse legitimate tokens across different services than intended. Token passthrough. If the MCP server not only accepts tokens with incorrect audiences but also forwards these unmodified tokens to downstream services, it can potentially cause the “confused deputy” problem, where the downstream API may incorrectly trust the token as if it came from the MCP server or assume the token was validated by the upstream API. Risks Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden in the authorization specification as it introduces a number of security risks, that include: Security Control Circumvention The MCP Server or downstream APIs might implement important security controls like rate limiting, request validation, or traffic monitoring, that depend on the token audience or other credential constraints. If clients can obtain and use tokens directly with the downstream APIs without the MCP server validating them properly or ensuring that the tokens are issued for the right service, they bypass these controls. Accountability and Audit Trail Issues The MCP Server will be unable to identify or distinguish between MCP Clients when clients are calling with an upstream-issued access token which may be opaque to the MCP Server. The downstream Resource Server’s logs may show requests that appear to

title: Security Best Practices
content: to come from a different source with a different identity, rather than the MCP server that is actually forwarding the tokens. Both factors make incident investigation, controls, and auditing more difficult. If the MCP Server passes tokens without validating their claims (e.g., roles, privileges, or audience) or other metadata, a malicious actor in possession of a stolen token can use the server as a proxy for data exfiltration. Trust Boundary Issues The downstream Resource Server grants trust to specific entities. This trust might include assumptions about origin or client behavior patterns. Breaking this trust boundary could lead to unexpected issues. If the token is accepted by multiple services without proper validation, an attacker compromising one service can use the token to access other connected services. Future Compatibility Risk Even if an MCP Server starts as a “pure proxy” today, it might need to add security controls later. Starting with proper token audience separation makes it easier to evolve the security model. Mitigation MCP servers MUST NOT accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server.

title: Security Best Practices
