title: Contributor Ladder
content: The contributor roles in the MCP project, what each requires and grants, and how people move between them. This page defines the contributor roles in the MCP project, what each requires and grants, and how people move between them. It was adopted by SEP-2148, a Specification Enhancement Proposal (SEP), and is changed by a Process SEP. Authority between roles is defined in Governance, and the group-level roles (WG Member, WG Lead, IG Facilitator) in Working Groups and Interest Groups.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Role What it is Access granted Minimum time Contributor Anyone who has contributed to MCP in any form None. Issues and group meetings are open to all. Pull requests vary by repository None Member Established, active contributor GitHub organization membership, triage rights 2-3 months of active participation Maintainer Steward of a named area (an SDK, a tool, a docs area, a group) Merge rights in the area, listed in MAINTAINERS.md 6 months as Member Core Maintainer Project-wide technical leadership; authority in Governance Administrative rights on all repositories By invitation after sustained Maintainer contribution Lead Maintainer Founding role; authority in Governance Administrative rights on all repositories and infrastructure Founders and their successors only Community Moderator Code of Conduct enforcement and incident handling Moderation tools on Discord and GitHub Discussions Member status; parallel track Timelines are minimums, advancement is discretionary, and an exception requires Core Maintainer approval with written rationale. Code, specification text, documentation, triage, security work, community work and moderation all count equally toward every role.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: A Contributor is anyone who has contributed to MCP in any form: issues, pull requests, group discussion, documentation, or help to others. There are no formal requirements. Start at Contributing and join the channels listed in Communication. Pull requests on the specification repository are opened by Members. Other repositories set their own rules in their contributing guides.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Requirements. Several contributions to MCP, including at least one merged pull request or accepted contribution. Ongoing engagement over 2-3 months rather than one-off contributions. Two-factor authentication enabled on GitHub. No objection from existing Members within 7 days of nomination. Sponsorship and approval. Sponsored by two Members or Maintainers from different organizations, or by one Core Maintainer or Lead Maintainer. Approved by no-objection. Duties. Respond to issues and pull requests assigned to you. Help onboard new contributors when you can. Follow the Code of Conduct. Privileges. GitHub organization membership with triage rights. Can be assigned issues and pull requests and use review commands such as /lgtm. Can open pull requests on the specification repository, as set out in Contributing. Eligible to serve as WG Lead or IG Facilitator. The member lists in the access repository are the roster. No separate list is published. Minimum time. 2-3 months of active participation.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Requirements. Six or more months as a Member with sustained contributions. Leadership or ownership of something concrete: an SDK, a tool, a documentation area, a working or interest group, or a significant initiative. Acting for the project over the interests of any employer. Knowledge of the roadmap, the design principles and how the area is used in practice. Completed security and governance onboarding. Sponsorship and approval. Sponsored by one Maintainer or Core Maintainer. Approved by Core Maintainers. Duties. Own the operational health of the area, including test stability, documentation currency, the release process and milestone planning. Review escalated decisions within the timelines under Escalation, and make sure proposals that reach Core Maintainers are refined and account for ecosystem-wide impact. Mentor Members and sponsor future Maintainers. Speak for the area’s users, represent MCP externally when asked, and take part in roadmap and governance discussions and in the project’s GitHub and Discord channels. Privileges. Merge rights in owned areas. May sponsor Members, Maintainers and SEPs (see SEP Guidelines). Included in roadmap and prioritization discussions. Listed in MAINTAINERS.md. Minimum time. 6 months as Member.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Requirements. Six or more months as a Maintainer or in equivalent standing. Demonstrated judgment on project-wide decisions. Trusted across organizations. Sponsorship and approval. Nominated by a majority of Core Maintainers and approved by Lead Maintainers, or appointed directly by Lead Maintainers. Removal is by Lead Maintainers (see Governance). Duties. Steward the design principles and the roadmap, and hold to long-term restraint in protocol evolution. Decide contested and cross-cutting technical questions and governance matters under the decision process. Represent the project externally, plan succession, and watch community health. Attend the Core Maintainer meeting every two weeks and Steering Group meetups. Privileges. Vote on SEPs and governance matters. Approve Maintainers, breaking changes and major specification revisions. Administrative rights on all MCP repositories. Listed in MAINTAINERS.md. Minimum time. By invitation after sustained Maintainer contribution. The group is kept small and delegates to Maintainers, WG Leads and IG Facilitators rather than growing. When evaluating candidates, Core Maintainers consider whether it reflects the breadth of MCP adoption, including enterprise adopters running MCP in production.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Lead Maintainer is the founding role, held for life, with no advancement path into it. A Lead Maintainer holds every Core Maintainer duty and privilege plus the powers listed in Governance (veto, appointment and removal of Core Maintainers, acting alone).

title: Contributor Ladder
content: If a Lead Maintainer leaves the role for any reason, succession begins on their written notice or, if they cannot give notice, when the remaining Lead Maintainers or the Core Maintainers determine that the Lead Maintainer is unable to continue serving. While one or more Lead Maintainers remain, they appoint the successor, by majority vote if more than one remains, and continue to govern until the successor is appointed. If no Lead Maintainers remain, the Core Maintainers appoint a successor by majority vote within 30 days, and the project operates by two-thirds vote of Core Maintainers until a new Lead Maintainer is appointed.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Requirements. Member status. Composure and good judgment in community interactions. Working knowledge of the Code of Conduct. Discretion and fairness in sensitive situations. Sponsorship and approval. Sponsored and approved by one Core Maintainer or Lead Maintainer. Core Maintainers may remove a moderator for failure to uphold moderation standards or for Code of Conduct violations. A moderator may step down at any time. Duties. Watch community channels, including Discord and GitHub Discussions, for Code of Conduct violations. Triage and respond to Code of Conduct reports, and escalate serious or complex incidents to Core Maintainers. Coordinate with other moderators so that enforcement is consistent. Record moderation actions and keep incident details confidential. Recuse from any incident you are party to. Those incidents go directly to Core Maintainers. Privileges. Moderation rights and tools on Discord and GitHub Discussions, and access to private moderator channels. May warn, mute or temporarily ban users for Code of Conduct violations. Listed in MAINTAINERS.md. Minimum time. None beyond Member status. Community Moderator is a parallel track that may be held alongside any other role and is not a prerequisite for technical advancement. Moderation work counts toward every role.

title: Contributor Ladder
header: Leading a working or interest group
content: WG Lead and IG Facilitator require Member status, not Maintainer status, and the work counts toward advancement to Maintainer. Their requirements, sponsorship and duties are defined in Working Groups and Interest Groups.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: You may nominate yourself or be nominated by a sponsor. Self-nominees still need the sponsors listed below. The nominee or a sponsor opens an issue in the specification repository using the nomination template, with links to the contributions that meet the role’s requirements. Sponsors confirm their support in the thread. A 7-day community comment period runs. The approving body decides and records the outcome in the thread. Access is provisioned through the access repository and the new role-holder completes onboarding. Role Sponsors Approved by Member 2 Members or Maintainers from different organizations, or 1 Core or Lead Maintainer No objection from existing Members within 7 days Maintainer 1 Maintainer or Core Maintainer Core Maintainers Core Maintainer Nominated by a majority of Core Maintainers Lead Maintainers, who may instead appoint directly Community Moderator 1 Core or Lead Maintainer The sponsoring Core or Lead Maintainer

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Decisions are made at the lowest level that owns the matter and are recorded in writing. Maintainers, WG Leads and IG Facilitators handle day-to-day decisions within their scope. Core Maintainers act on escalation, on cross-cutting questions, and where a process requires them, such as specification changes and Maintainer approval. Lead Maintainers act only on contested governance decisions or when Core Maintainers cannot reach a decision. Escalate only when you are blocked, when the decision has project-wide effect, or when a process on these pages requires it. Issue type First escalation Second escalation Response time Technical disagreement in a pull request Maintainer in scope Core Maintainer 5 business days Technical disagreement in a working group WG Lead Core Maintainer 5 business days Technical disagreement in an interest group IG Facilitator Core Maintainer 5 business days Disagreement with a WG Lead or IG Facilitator Core Maintainer Lead Maintainer 7 business days Disagreement with a Maintainer decision Core Maintainer Lead Maintainer 7 business days Disagreement among Core Maintainers Lead Maintainer None 10 business days Code of Conduct violation Community Moderator Core Maintainer Immediate Security issue Core Maintainer Lead Maintainer Immediate A vulnerability is reported through a private advisory first (see Reporting a vulnerability). The security row is the maintainer-internal escalation once a report exists. Maintainers who learn of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident must follow the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) escalation rule. They must notify a Core Maintainer or Lead Maintainer immediately in #security-disclosures on Discord while they fix the problem, and that Core Maintainer or Lead Maintainer works with the Linux Foundation CRA steward. To escalate: Document the decision, the options considered and the points of disagreement. Present it to the escalation authority with a clear ask. The escalation authority gives binding

title: Contributor Ladder
content: binding guidance, asks for more information, or escalates further. Disputes inside a working or interest group follow Working Groups and Interest Groups, which lists the disputes that go straight to Core Maintainers and requires that the Core Maintainer designated to resolve a group dispute share no organizational affiliation with the parties.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Members with no contributions for 3 months may be moved to emeritus status. Returning Members go through a simplified re-familiarization. Maintainers with no contributions for 6 months may be moved to emeritus status after Core Maintainer review, and the move revokes their merge rights. Returning Maintainers repeat the security and governance onboarding. Lead Maintainers review a Core Maintainer after 6 months without participation in governance or technical decisions and may move them to emeritus status. Core Maintainers should say early when their availability drops.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: You may step down from any role for any reason. Tell the WG Lead, IG Facilitator, Maintainer or Core Maintainer you work with, hand over open work, and move to emeritus status.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: Emeritus role-holders keep their recognition in MAINTAINERS.md and release notes and hold no duties or privileges.

title: Contributor Ladder
content: A role may be revoked for Code of Conduct violations or sustained non-participation, following appropriate review.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: The MCP project's working groups and interest groups, how to join or start one, and the operating rules every group follows. This page lists the project’s working groups and interest groups, explains how to join or start one, and sets the operating rules every group follows. The rules were adopted by SEP-2149, a Specification Enhancement Proposal (SEP). A group’s charter cannot override them, and changing them requires a Process SEP. Group membership is not required to take part in a group’s work, though a SEP needs prior discussion with the relevant working group and its agreement to sponsor before the pull request is marked ready for review. You may take part in as many groups as your time allows.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Working group Interest group Purpose Build a concrete solution Identify and discuss a problem Output SEPs, reference implementations, or stewardship of an endorsed project such as the Inspector, the Registry or an SDK Problem statements, use cases, recommendations, and input to working groups and SEPs Decisions Binding within scope: lazy consensus, then vote, then escalation Non-binding, by rough consensus Led by Leads Facilitators Duration Until its deliverables are complete Ongoing while the topic is relevant Example Transports Security In the usual path an interest group frames a problem, and a working group solves it. That can be an existing working group or a new one the interest group starts through the forming a group process, and the working group sponsors any resulting SEP.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Working groups: MCP Apps File Uploads Filesystems Governance Infrastructure Inspector V2 Interceptors Progressive Disclosure Registry SDK Server Card Skills Over MCP Tasks and Events Transports Interest groups: Agents Authorization Enterprise Financial Services Scientific Computing Security Tool Annotations

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Join the group’s Discord channel, which the charter names (Communication gives the naming convention). Attend the group’s call, listed on meet.modelcontextprotocol.io, and follow its agenda and notes thread (see Meetings and channels). Offering to take notes, prepare an agenda or facilitate a call is the fastest way in. Share your use cases in SEP discussions and take on working group deliverables when you are ready. To be listed as a Participant, ask a Lead. WG Member status follows the nomination process under Participation levels. Member lists live in the access repository, which drives GitHub team membership and Discord roles. The Antitrust Policy applies in every group meeting.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Each group has one or more Leads, called Facilitators in an interest group. A Lead or Facilitator must hold at least Member status and show sustained engagement with the group’s scope. They must be able to facilitate across organizations, represent several perspectives fairly, and commit to running the group’s operations; for a WG Lead that means 2 to 3 hours a week. The group and its leadership must be sponsored by at least two Core Maintainers or one Lead Maintainer. Every Lead and Facilitator must: schedule and run regular meetings under Meetings and channels set agendas with participants and publish them in advance make sure meeting notes are published keep the charter and other group documentation current keep the member list and access list in the access repository current recruit and retain a broad membership across organizations and perspectives A WG Lead must also: drive the group’s proposals through the SEP process to resolution triage SEPs in the group’s scope and close those that do not fit the roadmap, giving written rationale on the pull request; the author may appeal to Core Maintainers escalate blocked decisions to Core Maintainers with clear context keep the group’s roadmap (the charter’s Active Work Items) current and feed it into the project roadmap regularly check the group’s general direction with one or more Core Maintainers post the quarterly update under Reporting Leading a group does not require Maintainer status, and it counts toward advancement to Maintainer. A Lead or Facilitator who is not a Maintainer works with one for merge decisions. Lead authority covers group operations, not specification approval. A WG Lead may sponsor SEPs within the group’s scope.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Level Description Privileges Observer Anyone interested in following the group’s work Read access, may attend meetings, limited discussion participation Participant Active contributor to group discussions Can propose agenda items, participate in async votes WG Member Sustained contributor with demonstrated expertise Counted for quorum (WGs only) Lead/Facilitator Operational leadership of the group Sets agenda, facilitates, escalates WG Member is a group-level tier distinct from the project-wide Member role: a person may be a WG Member without holding Member status, and the reverse. Interest groups primarily operate with Observers, Participants and Facilitators, and may adopt the WG Member tier if their work warrants formal decision-making. In a working group, or an interest group that has adopted the tier, becoming a WG Member requires three things: sustained participation over 3 months with contributions of code, specification text, reviews or documentation; nomination by an existing WG Member or Lead; and no objection from the Leads, Core Maintainers or Lead Maintainers within 7 days. WG Members keep their name, organization and Discord handle current in the group’s member list. A WG Member who does not participate for 3 consecutive months is moved to emeritus status and may return by demonstrating renewed participation.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Working groups make binding decisions within their scope through three steps, each attempted before the next. Lazy consensus. A proposal is announced with a clear deadline of at least 5 days for minor items and 10 days for significant items. Silence is consent. Any WG Member may block with a documented objection, which must propose alternatives or clear criteria for resolution. If no block is raised by the deadline, the proposal is accepted. Formal vote. A vote is triggered when a WG Member blocks during the lazy consensus period, or when a Lead or three or more WG Members request one. Quorum is 50% of active WG Members. Routine matters pass by simple majority and scope changes by a two-thirds majority. Core Maintainer feedback is advisory unless explicitly stated as binding. Every vote is documented with rationale. Escalation. If the vote fails to resolve the matter (no quorum, no passage, or a contested result), the Lead escalates to Core Maintainers under Escalation. Interest groups operate by rough consensus and their output is non-binding. An interest group that has adopted the WG Member tier may use these steps for internal decisions. Each working group’s charter records, in its Authority and Decision Rights table, the decisions the group takes at each level. That table is approved with the charter and changed under Amending or retiring a group.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: The generic escalation procedure and response-time matrix are defined in the Contributor Ladder. Technical and design disagreements within a group’s scope are resolved in the group before Core Maintainers are involved: a working group uses Making decisions, and an interest group’s Facilitator seeks rough consensus. Scope disputes (whether a topic falls within the charter), authority disputes (whether the group may decide a matter), cross-group conflicts, Code of Conduct or behavioral concerns, and membership or participation disputes should be escalated directly to Core Maintainers. When a Lead escalates, the Core Maintainer group designates one of its members, who should not share organizational affiliation with the parties involved, to resolve the issue and report back to the group. That Core Maintainer provides binding guidance, requests more information, or recommends that the full Core Maintainer group deliberate. An escalation should receive an initial response within 5 business days.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Leads set each group’s meeting frequency, format and duration; there is no fixed cadence. Every group meeting must: be open to all community participants, with no closed or organization-internal meetings be published on meet.modelcontextprotocol.io at least 7 days in advance have a public agenda; the agenda or a link to it should be posted as a GitHub Discussion in the Meeting Notes category before the meeting have its notes published to the same discussion within 48 hours use the official Google Meet transcription as its only automated record; third-party AI notetakers and meeting bots are not permitted, per the Code of Conduct run under the Code of Conduct and the Antitrust Policy, whose Conduct of Meetings section requires agendas and minutes link Project Policies from its agenda Leads should involve WG Members and Participants in preparing agendas, taking notes and facilitating. Each group has a Discord channel (naming at Communication) for quick questions and coordination; responses there are best effort. Long-form technical discussion goes to GitHub Discussions, which are triaged weekly, and a group may have its own Discussions category on request. Leads are granted the roles needed to manage and moderate both.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Each working group posts a quarterly update at the end of January, April, July and October as a document in its GitHub Discussions category, covering progress against deliverables, blocked items and escalations, membership changes, upcoming priorities, and resource needs. Core Maintainers may take it up at their meeting. Interest groups have no reporting requirement but should keep their charter and member list current.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: A working group is formed when a widely acknowledged problem needs coordinated work. Prior discussion in an interest group helps but is not required. With a clear deliverable you may propose a working group directly. The group and its Leads need the sponsorship set out under Leadership; ask in the Discord channel closest to the topic or in #wg-ig-group-creation. Once sponsored, the proposers submit a charter as described in Submitting a charter. The WG Lead approves the initial member list.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: Fill out the creation template in the #wg-ig-group-creation channel on Discord. A Core Maintainer reviews the proposal, and the group and its Facilitators need the same sponsorship. Once sponsored, the Facilitators organize the group and submit a charter the same way, with the file under docs/community/interest-groups/.

title: Working Groups and Interest Groups
content: A change to a group’s charter is proposed by a Lead, a Facilitator or a Core Maintainer, approved by Core Maintainers, and recorded in the charter’s Changelog. A working group is retired when its Lead or a Core Maintainer proposes retirement with rationale and a Core Maintainer or Lead Maintainer approves. It is also retired when it has completed all planned deliverables or has had no active work for a sustained period. Core Maintainers or Lead Maintainers may retire an interest group that is no longer active or needed. In both cases the group’s documentation is archived and its channels are marked inactive.

title: Group Charter Template
content: The charter template for MCP working groups and interest groups, and how to submit a charter. This page gives the charter template that every working group and interest group must follow and explains how to submit a charter. The template was adopted by SEP-2149, a Specification Enhancement Proposal (SEP), and is changed, together with the rules in Working Groups and Interest Groups, by a Process SEP. Each charter lives at docs/community/working-groups/<name>.mdx or docs/community/interest-groups/<name>.mdx in the modelcontextprotocol repository, records only the group’s mission, scope, leadership, membership and operations, and does not restate those rules, which apply to every group. Sections marked (WG only) are required for working groups and optional for interest groups. To start a group, see Forming a group.

title: Group Charter Template
content: The group must already be sponsored under Forming a group. Copy the template below into the charter file and replace the placeholders. Delete the {/* */} guidance comments or leave them as written: HTML comments break the MDX build, and npm run format corrupts a {/* */} comment that spans lines. Run npm run prep, then push. Open a pull request that adds the charter file, a navigation entry under Working Groups or Interest Groups in docs/docs.json, and a line under Current groups. A Core Maintainer will review the pull request, as outlined in the Amending or retiring a group requirements. Later changes follow Amending or retiring a group and add a row to the charter’s Changelog. Transports and Security are filled-in examples, for a working group and an interest group respectively.

title: MCP Apps Working Group Charter
content: The MCP Apps Working Group defines, evolves, and maintains the official extension for interactive user interfaces over MCP. The working group oversees the extension specification, SDK, reference implementations, security model, conformance work, and guidance so that apps can run safely and consistently across independent MCP hosts.

title: MCP Apps Working Group Charter
content: Specification Work: The MCP Apps extension specification and related SEPs, covering the areas below under the io.modelcontextprotocol/ui namespace. App Lifecycle: How apps are declared, initialized, persisted, and torn down, including UI resource declaration and tool metadata. App Interaction Model: The interaction protocol between user, app, and host, such as bi-directional messaging, app tools, etc. Content Types and Rendering Targets: Support for different content types and methodologies like generative UI, with interoperability with external protocols such as A2UI and AG-UI. Security Model: The threat model, sandboxing, security policy, permissions, and auditability of UI-initiated actions. SDKs and Reference Implementations: The @modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps SDK, reference host, example servers, and host integration examples. Conformance: Compatibility tests, app validation, and the definition of conformance requirements for apps and hosts. Cross-Cutting Coordination: App discovery and metadata (with the Registry WG), UI in agentic flows (with the Agents IG), and per-language SDK support (with the SDK WG). Documentation: API references, authoring guidance, host integration guidance, starter resources, and examples.

title: MCP Apps Working Group Charter
content: Core protocol ownership: Changes to base MCP semantics, transports, or lifecycle are proposed through the SEP process and owned by the relevant group or Core Maintainers. Host-specific product and design decisions: Hosts control their user experience and visual design. The WG standardizes the interoperability and security contract. Individual app implementations: Apps built on the extension remain the responsibility of their authors. General agent orchestration: Agent loops and sub-agent coordination belong to the Agents IG, and task management belongs to the Tasks and Events WG. This WG covers only the interactive UI surface and its integration points.

title: MCP Apps Working Group Charter
content: Agents IG: Interactive UI within agentic flows and task lifecycles. Registry WG: App discovery, distribution, and metadata. Security IG: Sandboxing, permissions, and review of UI-initiated actions. SDK WG: SDK consistency and support outside the TypeScript reference implementation.

title: File Uploads Charter
content: The File Uploads Working Group exists to define how MCP tools and elicitation requests declare file inputs so that hosts can present native file pickers and pass user-selected file content to servers. Today, servers that need a file from the user resort to prose instructions asking for base64 strings or local paths, which produces inconsistent UX and pushes encoding details onto end users. This WG will specify a minimal, schema-level mechanism for declaring file inputs and the wire format for delivering them, anchored on SEP-2356. As a secondary goal, the WG covers how a tool returns a file that is too large for a JSON-RPC message or that needs authorization to fetch.

title: File Uploads Charter
content: Specification Work: SEPs defining declarative file input descriptors on tool input schemas and elicitation request schemas, the wire encoding for file content, and host-side handling requirements. File Downloads (secondary): How a tool returns a file that is too large for a JSON-RPC message or that needs authorization to fetch. Upload work takes priority. Reference Implementations: SDK types and helpers for FileInputDescriptor, data URI encoding, and a sample host flow demonstrating picker invocation and value substitution. Cross-Cutting Concerns: Coordination with the MCP Apps WG where embedded UI surfaces present their own file pickers, and with the Security IG on host-side validation requirements. Documentation: Specification sections covering file input declaration and a migration guide for servers currently using ad-hoc base64 instructions.

title: File Uploads Charter
content: Server-to-client delivery of small files, which Resources and BlobResourceContents already cover. Changes to the transport layer or session model. The WG may evaluate approaches such as streaming, chunked transfer, or presigned upload URLs as part of its design work; whether those land in the initial SEP or a follow-up is a WG decision rather than a charter constraint.

title: File Uploads Charter
content: MCP Apps WG — embedded app UIs may surface their own file pickers; the descriptor format should be reusable in that context. Security IG — host-side validation requirements for user-supplied file content (the SEP references OWASP ASVS V5 for general upload hygiene). Tool Annotations IG — file input descriptors are a form of input-parameter metadata and should remain consistent with the broader annotation taxonomy.

title: Filesystems Charter
content: Working Group

title: Filesystems Charter
content: The Filesystems Working Group exists to align MCP Resources with general filesystem semantics, so that MCP clients have one interface for discovering, retrieving and modifying filesystem-shaped resources across sources, and can do so efficiently. Agent platforms are converging on presenting services to models as filesystems, and Resources already addresses content by URI under a file:// scheme the specification defines as identifying “resources that behave like a filesystem”. The WG will determine which filesystem semantics fit MCP and produce one or more Extensions Track SEPs that apply those semantics consistently to Resources.

title: Filesystems Charter
content: Specification Work: One or more Extensions Track SEPs defining resource operations, covering: Scoped listing and directory traversal. Investigate hierarchy-aware listing scoped to a URI, including an operation that enumerates one level below a URI, analogous to readdir, traversal of a whole subtree, and how both relate to the existing flat resources/list operation. Server-side search. Investigate search and glob matching evaluated by the server, so a client can find content without listing and reading every resource. This goes beyond resource templates, which describe the URIs a server accepts. Together with scoped listing and traversal, this covers how a client discovers content on a server. Read semantics. Investigate which filesystem read semantics fit MCP, including bulk reads of several URIs in one request and whether the protocol can support a seek operation. Write and metadata operations. Define create, update, delete, and a metadata read (stat) that answers existence, size and last-modified for one URI without fetching the body. Optimistic concurrency control. Specify how two writers avoid a lost update, and how a client creates a resource under a create-if-absent precondition. Typed errors. Define errors for resource operations, e.g. not found, already exists, precondition failed and permission denied, so a client handles a failure the same way across servers. Currently, a missing resource returns the generic -32602 (Invalid Params). Change notification and caching. Specify how filesystem operations interact with notifications/resources/updated, the time-to-live and cache scope fields ttlMs and cacheScope, and the lastModified annotation. Cross-Cutting Concerns: Reconcile the proposals that extend this primitive into one coherent design. SEP-2571, Resource Submission for Agent Coordination proposes resources/create and resources/delete. SEP-2532, Resource Streaming for Binary Content Delivery proposes resources/stream. SEP-1708, MCP Client-Brokered

title: Filesystems Charter
content: Client-Brokered Filesystem Access proposed a files/* method family standing beside Resources, and closed on 23 January 2026. Documentation: Document the adopted filesystem semantics in the specification, and give server authors guidance on choosing between a resource operation and a tool-based one.

title: Filesystems Charter
content: A parallel files/* primitive standing beside Resources. The WG broadens the existing Resources primitive. A complete mapping of POSIX or another operating system’s filesystem API. The WG will select the semantics that fit a client-server protocol and document the rationale for any exclusions. Host-side sandbox and local-disk semantics. The WG standardizes the client and server wire format. How a host materializes resources into a filesystem for the model stays a host concern. Authorization policy for filesystem operations, beyond stating where the existing MCP authorization specification applies.

title: Filesystems Charter
content: File Uploads WG. Both groups transfer content to a server. Coordination is needed on where an upload-oriented flow ends and a resource write operation begins. Discovery, search, metadata and small inline writes do not depend on large-content transfer, and can progress independently of it. Tools already return resource links, so the groups should also agree on whether a tool input that takes a file can take a reference to a Resource. Skills Over MCP WG. The published Skills extension uses Resources for file reads and defines optional directory reading. It does not depend on filesystem write operations; coordinate on future resource operations that affect skills. Agents IG. Multi-agent and job orchestration systems are the motivating consumers of shared filesystem semantics.

title: Governance Working Group Charter
content: Charter for the MCP Governance Working Group.

title: Governance Working Group Charter
content: Working Group

title: Governance Working Group Charter
content: The Governance Working Group exists to refine, document, and steward MCP’s governance processes and community values, providing a single home for revising the project’s governance documentation as the project grows. It also serves as an advisory voice channel — surfacing community concerns to Core Maintainers and stewarding the contribution culture that helps people advance through the contributor ladder. Over time the WG aspires to evolve into a standing consultation forum for contested governance decisions and, longer-term, to support representative community participation in the broader MCP organization.

title: Governance Working Group Charter
content: Governance Documentation Stewardship: Content under docs/community/ covering governance, contributor-ladder, sep-guidelines, working-interest-groups, communication, antitrust, and project policies. Editorial revisions land autonomously; substantive revisions go through WG consensus and Core Maintainer approval (see Authority & Decision Rights below). Pages with an owner assigned outside this WG, and the WG and IG charter pages gated to Core Maintainers by CODEOWNERS, are subject to tighter collaboration with the owner: the WG proposes changes to those; it does not land them. Decision Recording: Defining what counts as a project decision, who ratifies it, and how it is recorded across meeting notes, GitHub Discussions, and the SEP record. Code of Conduct Stewardship: Drafting, revising, and maintaining the Code of Conduct text and adjacent reporting/escalation documentation. Content revisions go through WG consensus → Core Maintainer approval. Community Values: Stewardship of MCP’s stated community values, including landing the in-progress values workshop as a public artefact under docs/community/. Contribution Culture & Mentorship: Encouraging mentorship as a culture (not a formal pairings program in v0.1) and stewarding practice for movement across the contributor ladder tiers, in coordination with SEP-2148. Voice Channel: Surfacing community concerns from contributors and observers to Core Maintainers in an advisory, non-binding capacity. Concerns arrive in #governance-wg or at the monthly working session; the Lead carries those needing Core Maintainer attention to the monthly Core Maintainer plus WG/IG leads meeting. Cross-Cutting Coordination: Coordination with other WGs and IGs on governance processes that affect them. The WG sets the framework; per-group operations remain with the groups themselves.

title: Governance Working Group Charter
content: Specification authorship: Protocol changes go through the SEP process and the relevant spec-producing Working Group. The Governance WG never owns spec sections. It may sponsor a SEP that changes a governance process. Maintainer selection and succession: Lead Maintainers appoint Core Maintainers; Core Maintainers approve Maintainers. The WG may recommend process improvements but does not pick people. Individual Code of Conduct moderation decisions: Receipt, investigation, and adjudication of individual incident reports are not within this WG’s purview. The WG’s near-term goal is to receive aggregated, anonymized trend reports from whoever performs incident handling, to inform policy revision. Per-SDK governance: Owned by the SDK Working Group. Per-WG/IG internal operations: Each group runs its own meetings, prioritisation, and member coordination; the Governance WG sets framework only. Maintainer disputes and interpersonal conflict resolution outside the Code of Conduct: Explicitly out of scope for v0.1. Scoping a possible escalation path is a candidate future deliverable; claiming the role itself is not.

title: Governance Working Group Charter
content: Core Maintainers — material governance changes, Code of Conduct content revisions, and contributor ladder structural changes require Core Maintainer approval. The Lead represents the WG at the monthly Core Maintainer plus WG/IG leads meeting and surfaces community concerns there in an advisory capacity. All other Working Groups and Interest Groups — the WG sets the governance framework that all groups inherit (charter template, decision rights, meeting requirements). Per-group operations remain with the groups themselves. Interest groups route governance questions here. SDK Working Group — coordination on the boundary between project-wide governance and per-SDK governance, which lives there. Future Code of Conduct handling body — once the CoC reporting/handling path is formalised, the body that handles individual incidents will share aggregated, anonymised trend reports with the WG to inform policy revision.

title: Infrastructure Charter
content: The Infrastructure Working Group builds and maintains MCP’s shared infrastructure and automation. It makes routine administration self-service for maintainers and contributors. Governance defines who can do what; Infra implements those decisions through standard tools and workflows.

title: Infrastructure Charter
content: Access and accounts: Organization invitations, team membership, permissions, and account provisioning. This includes letting authorized leads of MCP working groups invite contributors to the organization and manage access for their own groups, including contributors who cannot yet open pull requests. GitHub administration: Creating and configuring repositories, managing teams and access, and automating common administrative tasks. Group setup: Setting up repositories, permissions, email, meetings, and other resources for approved MCP groups. Meetings and communication: Google Workspace accounts, aliases, mailing lists, calendars, scheduling, agendas, and notifications. Discord integrations and MCP bridges for important project events. Shared services: Improving MCP’s planning, voting, and meeting services with their current owners. Hosting and publishing: Websites, documentation hosting, CI/CD, deployment, package publishing access, domains, DNS, and certificates. Supporting resources: Compute, storage, credentials, and other infrastructure MCP needs now or adopts later. Maintenance: Monitoring, upgrades, recovery, ownership changes, and removal of unused resources. The Infrastructure WG should start with gaps and repeated manual work. Infrastructure that works well should stay in place. Changes to an existing setup or its ownership should be agreed with its owners. The Infrastructure WG should build on existing repositories and tools. Shared workflows should make resources easy to create, manage, and remove. Configuration and changes should be recorded so they can be reviewed and reproduced.

title: Infrastructure Charter
content: Setting governance policy, deciding who holds a role, or changing approval requirements. Setting voting rules, moderation policy, or communications policy. Protocol and SDK design, release decisions, website content, and other groups’ roadmaps. Taking over services or requiring migrations without agreement from their owners. Infrastructure for individuals, companies, or third-party MCP deployments.

title: Infrastructure Charter
content: SDK WG and SDK maintainers: The Infrastructure WG provides shared tools for repository setup, access, CI, and publishing. SDK maintainers keep responsibility for their SDKs and releases. Other WGs and IGs: The Infrastructure WG provides tools for group setup, membership, communication, and infrastructure. Each group keeps responsibility for its work and services.

title: Interceptors Charter
content: Charter for the MCP Interceptors Working Group.

title: Interceptors Charter
content: Working Group

title: Interceptors Charter
content: The Interceptors Working Group exists to standardize how context operations are intercepted, validated, and transformed at key points in the agentic lifecycle. This covers MCP-defined operations such as tool invocations, resource access, prompt handling, sampling, and elicitation, as well as any other operation that shapes agent context — including LLM completions and custom application-specific workflows. The ecosystem is developing a sprawling landscape of sidecars, proxies, and gateways for cross-cutting concerns that are largely non-reusable and non-interoperable, creating an M × N integration problem. The WG will produce specification extensions and reference implementations that define interceptors as a new MCP primitive with two types — validators (inspect and return pass/fail decisions) and mutators (transform context payloads) — discoverable and invocable through MCP’s existing JSON-RPC patterns across deployment models including in-process, sidecar, and remote service.

title: Interceptors Charter
content: Specification Work: SEPs defining the interceptor primitive — validator and mutator types, lifecycle event hooks for MCP operations (tool calls, resource reads, prompt gets, sampling, elicitation) and extensible to non-MCP context operations (LLM completions, custom workflows), trust-boundary-aware execution model, priority-based chain ordering, and audit mode semantics. Reference Implementations: Multi-language SDK libraries for building interceptors, sample interceptors (PII redaction, schema validation, audit logging), a common interceptor sidecar/proxy runtime, and a CLI client for interceptor invocation and testing. Cross-Cutting Concerns: Transport-level interception points, gateway-based deployment patterns, and interplay with routing and policy layers (see Related Groups). Documentation: Specification sections covering interceptor authoring, deployment models (in-process, sidecar, remote service), chain configuration, and migration guidance from ad-hoc middleware approaches.

title: Interceptors Charter
content: Client-specific hook implementation details (e.g., Claude Code’s internal hook execution engine) — the WG standardizes the protocol-level interface, not host internals. Transport-layer wire format or session model changes (owned by the Transports WG). General-purpose middleware or proxy infrastructure beyond what the MCP protocol requires.

title: Interceptors Charter
content: Transports WG — interceptors operate on MCP message flows whose delivery behavior depends on the transport; coordination needed on transport-level interception points. Gateways IG — gateways are a key deployment model for interceptors; coordination needed on gateway-based interceptor patterns and shared concerns around routing, policy, and observability.

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Working Group

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: The Progressive Disclosure Working Group explores how MCP Primitives (Tools, Resources, Prompts, Tasks) might be organized, beyond the flat lists maintained by the protocol, and how such organization might benefit both MCP servers and clients. The group documents diverse requirements from clients, servers, and gateways, supports reference extensions of varied organization strategies, and feeds recommendations into the SEP process rather than picking a single canonical pattern early.

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Requirements gathering: documenting use cases and constraints Pattern exploration: testing and evaluating various approaches Proof of concepts: maintaining a shared repository of reference implementations and experimental findings

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Approving spec changes: this WG does not have authority to approve protocol changes; recommendations flow through the SEP process Implementation mandates: the group can document patterns but cannot require specific client or server behavior

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Tool Annotations IG - annotation-based filtering and selection of primitives intersects with how primitives are organized and surfaced Skills Over MCP WG - maintains the published Skills extension; skill discovery and progressive disclosure overlap with grouping

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Flat lists of MCP primitives can be long and cumbersome to work with for several reasons. Many such problems are within the scope of this group, but some are not. Within Scope Context overload - when loaded into the context of an LLM, a primitive list can overwhelm the model and lead to confusion and poor selection Inefficient operations - long lists in the context consume many tokens, which increases processing cost and response latency Poor developer experience - the lack of organizational tools for primitives makes them harder to manage and maintain Beyond Scope Organization for security - organizing and disclosing primitives to clients based on their privilege level is an important problem but beyond this group’s mandate Organizing MCP servers - server discovery and registry schema decisions belong to the Registry WG, with skill-distribution requirements contributed by the Skills Over MCP WG

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Documenting requirements and experiences - document diverse requirements for the different clients, servers, and gateways that implement these extensions. We will not try to find consensus early on, but aim to document the trade-offs based on feedback from real-world experience. Reference extensions - many possible organization mechanisms are emerging, and it may be too early to select one canonical pattern. Different servers are implementing similar features, but the lack of standardization limits clients’ ability to leverage them effectively. This group will support reference extensions of varied organization strategies, e.g., grouping, tool-search, code-mode. Evangelizing standards - invite feedback from developers and maintainers of large MCP servers and clients to migrate away from bespoke implementations toward standardized extensions.

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: See Approaches for detailed descriptions of each strategy, including prior art, examples, and discussion links.

title: Progressive Disclosure Charter
content: Document discussions - the WG aims to document the trade-offs and discussions rather than dictate one specific implementation. Prefer GitHub Discussions on the WG repository over prolonged Discord threads. Meeting notes from synchronous WG calls are also uploaded to GitHub Discussions for future reference. Experimental extensions - the repository houses experimental extensions for different approaches. Extensions SHOULD support at least Python and TypeScript implementations and include (1) end-to-end working demonstrations and (2) detailed instructions for how others can integrate with them. Feedback from deployments - the WG solicits deployment experiences and feedback from users of extensions to prioritize feature development and changes.

content: Working Group

title: Registry Charter
content: The Registry Working Group exists to build and maintain the official MCP Registry — an open catalog and API for publicly available MCP servers — so that clients, sub-registries, and end users can discover, evaluate, and install servers with confidence. The WG owns the registry service, the server.json schema, the registry API specification, and the sub-registry ecosystem that further distributes server metadata.

title: Registry Charter
content: Registry Service: Operation, reliability, and evolution of the hosted registry at registry.modelcontextprotocol.io, including uptime, monitoring, and incident response. Registry API Specification: The OpenAPI spec defining how any registry (official or private) exposes server metadata. server.json Schema: The standardized format for describing MCP server identity, packages, runtime configuration, and capabilities — coordinated with the Server Card WG to keep Server Card a coherent subset. Client SDKs: Generated or hand-maintained client libraries that make it easy for clients and sub-registries to integrate with the registry API. Publishing & Trust: Authentication flows (GitHub OAuth, GitHub OIDC, DNS/HTTP verification), namespace ownership, moderation tooling, and community-driven flagging. Adoption & Outreach: Documentation, onboarding guides, and outreach to drive catalog coverage. Issue Triage & Automation: Labeling system, triage, and contributor workflow for the registry repo.

title: Registry Charter
content: Any runtime-related MCP protocol specification aspects (owned by Core Maintainers and other WGs). Server Card format and discovery mechanism (owned by the Server Card WG; this WG coordinates on server.json alignment). Ranking/choosing between MCP server implementations on behalf of MCP clients or end-users. Hosting, distributing, or executing MCP server code or binaries — the registry is a metadata catalog, not a package registry. Any commitment to delivering an enterprise-ready or reusable registry implementation. The codebase supports this instance only and is not intended for external deployments.

title: Registry Charter
content: Server Card WG — server.json and Server Card must stay aligned; the registry will expose Server Cards + local package-related metadata for published entries. Tight coordination required to avoid schema divergence.

content: The SDK Working Group exists to keep the official MCP SDKs consistent, conformant, and current with the specification. It coordinates implementation of new protocol versions across languages, governs the SDK Tiering System, and establishes shared design patterns where sensible, so that developers get a coherent experience across SDKs while each remains idiomatic to its language.

title: SDK Working Group Charter
content: SDK Tiering: Operating the SDK Tiering System, including reviewing tier advancement requests, applying relegation criteria, and maintaining the published tier assignments. Official SDK Roster: Evaluating proposals to add new official SDKs or retire existing ones. Release Coordination: Aligning Tier-1 SDK release plans with specification version dates so that protocol features land in SDKs on the timelines their tier requires. Cross-SDK Design Guidance: Recommending common patterns for SDK API surface, versioning, deprecation, error handling, and extension packaging, so that SDKs remain recognisably similar across languages while staying idiomatic. Conformance Integration: Working with the Conformance Testing project to ensure each official SDK runs the conformance suite and publishes results. Maintainer Coordination: Providing a forum for per-language SDK maintainers to share implementation experience and surface specification ambiguities back to Core Maintainers.

title: SDK Working Group Charter
content: Per-SDK day-to-day maintenance: Issue triage, PR review, and releases for an individual SDK remain the responsibility of that SDK’s maintainers as listed in MAINTAINERS.md. Specification authorship: Protocol changes are proposed through the SEP process and owned by the relevant working group or Core Maintainers. The SDK WG implements accepted SEPs; it does not own spec sections. Conformance test authoring: The conformance test suite itself is owned by the Conformance Testing project. Third-party and community SDKs: SDKs outside the modelcontextprotocol organization are not governed by this group.

title: SDK Working Group Charter
content: Transports WG: Transport implementations are a substantial part of every SDK. The SDK WG coordinates with the Transports WG on rollout sequencing when transport SEPs land. Conformance Testing: Tier assignments depend on conformance scores. The SDK WG consumes conformance results and feeds back gaps in test coverage. All specification-producing WGs: The SDK WG is a downstream consumer of accepted SEPs and coordinates reference-implementation timing with the originating group.

title: Tasks and Events Charter
content: Working Group

title: Tasks and Events Charter
content: The Tasks and Events Working Group exists to continue the development of Tasks, MCP’s existing foundation for durable asynchronous execution, and to define how servers proactively notify clients of state changes. Today, clients learn about server-side updates by polling or holding an SSE connection open. This WG will specify a standardized callback mechanism—webhooks or similar—that lets servers push notifications when new data is available, with defined ordering guarantees that hold across all transports.

title: Tasks and Events Charter
content: Tasks: Stabilization of the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension and its promotion into the core MCP protocol, including collecting implementation feedback, resolving ambiguities, and evaluating proposed changes to its lifecycle. Specification Work: SEPs defining the trigger/callback mechanism, subscription lifecycle, delivery semantics, and event ordering guarantees. Reference Implementations: SDK components demonstrating server-initiated notifications and client-side callback handling. Cross-Cutting Concerns: Coordination with the Transports WG on transport-specific delivery behavior, and with the Agents IG on agent-backed use cases that depend on Tasks or event triggers. Documentation: The Tasks specification, and specification sections covering event-driven patterns and migration guidance from polling-based approaches.

title: Tasks and Events Charter
content: Changes to the transport wire format or session model (owned by the Transports WG). General-purpose pub/sub infrastructure beyond what the MCP protocol requires. Modifications to existing notification primitives (notifications/resources/updated, notifications/tools/list_changed, etc.) that do not relate to proactive server-initiated delivery. Evaluation of agent-backed MCP use cases and of a possible Agents Extension, which belongs to the Agents IG.

title: Tasks and Events Charter
content: Transports WG — delivery and ordering guarantees depend on transport capabilities; callback semantics must be coherent across stdio, Streamable HTTP, and future transports. Agents IG — agent-as-tool, remote-agent, and supervisor/sub-agent patterns depend on Tasks and on task completion notifications. The IG provides use cases and requirements, and this WG owns the protocol surface.

title: Transports Charter
content: Charter for the MCP Transports Working Group.

title: Transports Charter
content: Working Group

title: Transports Charter
content: The Transports Working Group evolves MCP transport bindings and transport-adjacent protocol architecture so implementations remain interoperable, scalable, reliable, and easy to operate across local and remote deployments. The WG produces transport proposals, SEPs, implementation evidence, and guidance. The working group repository maintains the WG’s current technical focus, proposal strategy, and supporting detail within these boundaries.

title: Transports Charter
content: Transport Bindings: Framing, delivery, request and envelope metadata, cancellation and termination, connection lifecycle, backward compatibility, and the behavior of existing and future MCP transports. The current specification’s transport overview defines the boundary between a transport binding and core protocol semantics. Scalability and Reliability: Transport-level connection management, resource efficiency, multiplexing, load distribution, error handling, reconnection, resumption, and the delivery and ordering guarantees offered by a binding. Transport-Adjacent Protocol Architecture: Protocol-wide message-flow concerns required for scalable, interoperable bindings, including request association, per-request metadata, stateless operation, and migration from legacy initialization and transport-session models. Transport Security: Binding and envelope security requirements such as Origin validation, TLS, mTLS, and certificate handling, coordinated with the Security IG. Credential carriage is coordinated with the Auth IG. Validation and Guidance: Reference implementations, experiments, implementation evidence, and documentation needed to evaluate proposals and help implementers adopt agreed transport behavior. Supporting material is maintained in the upstream proposals directory. The WG contributes transport scenarios and requirements to the Conformance Testing project, whose maintainers own the conformance suite. Cross-Cutting Coordination: Transport implications of work owned by other MCP groups, without taking ownership of their application-layer features. The upstream mission statement provides supporting context but cannot expand the boundaries in this charter.

title: Transports Charter
content: Application-layer behavior for MCP primitives such as tools, resources, prompts, tasks, agents, or events, including application state, application-session meaning, task lifecycle, and event or subscription semantics. The WG coordinates where those features depend on binding or message-flow behavior. Domain-specific extensions and implementation-specific product or business concerns. SDK APIs and implementation details unrelated to transports. Authorization protocol mechanics, credential and token semantics, application identity, and authorization policy. The WG coordinates with the relevant groups on how bindings carry agreed authorization data. Ownership of the MCP conformance suite. The WG contributes transport requirements and scenarios in coordination with its maintainers.

title: Transports Charter
content: SDK WG: Official SDKs implement transport changes; the groups coordinate on feasibility, reference implementations, and rollout sequencing. Tasks and Events WG: The Tasks and Events WG owns Tasks and durable execution; the groups coordinate where these depend on multi-round-trip requests, request association, stateless operation, or binding behavior. Event callbacks, subscriptions, and application-level delivery semantics are owned by that group; Transports owns binding-specific carriage and guarantees. Auth IG and Security IG: The groups coordinate on credential carriage and transport wire security while authorization mechanics and broader security requirements remain with the respective IGs.

title: Agents Charter
content: Charter for the MCP Agents Interest Group.

title: Agents Charter
content: Interest Group

title: Agents Charter
content: The Agents Interest Group exists to make interactions with agent-backed systems interoperable over MCP. Today, these systems are typically exposed as ordinary tools or through framework-specific integrations, leaving durable execution, capability discovery, delegation, and multi-turn interaction to ad hoc conventions. The IG evaluates which remaining gaps require protocol support. Based on production use cases and prototypes, the group will recommend how to evolve the protocol, create additional extensions or document how existing MCP primitives should be used consistently.

title: Agents Charter
content: Agents Extension Evaluation: Evaluate agent-backed MCP use cases, including agent-as-tool, remote-agent, and supervisor/sub-agent patterns, to determine whether an Agents Extension is needed to complement Tasks. Prototypes and Proposals: Develop narrowly scoped proofs of concept where they help determine whether to introduce an Agents Extension, evolve Tasks, or rely on existing MCP primitives. Cross-Cutting Concerns: Coordinate with relevant groups when evaluated agent use cases raise tasks, transport, events, skills, authorization, metadata, or external-interoperability questions. Documentation: Document agent-backed MCP use cases, findings, and any recommendations produced by the group.

title: Agents Charter
content: Building or standardizing general-purpose agent frameworks and runtimes, including internal choices about planning, memory, model selection, and orchestration. The group focuses on behavior at MCP interoperability boundaries rather than host or server implementation internals. Transport wire formats and session mechanics, which are owned by the Transports WG. Tasks, general event delivery, and callback mechanisms, which are owned by the Tasks and Events WG. The charter does not predetermine where inference or agent loops run, or whether a particular capability belongs in Tasks, an Agents Extension, or existing MCP primitives. The IG evaluates those questions through its discussions.

title: Agents Charter
content: Transports WG - Task polling, multi-round-trip requests, stateless operation, and request association depend on transport and message-flow semantics. Tasks and Events WG - Tasks and proactive task-status and completion notifications are owned by that group. The IG provides use cases and requirements as input.

title: Authorization Charter
content: Charter for the MCP Authorization Interest Group.

title: Authorization Charter
content: Interest Group

title: Authorization Charter
content: The Authorization Interest Group is the single chartered venue for MCP authorization work. It brings MCP implementers, identity-provider vendors, and security practitioners together to surface real-world authorization problems, decide whether they are worth solving and whether they belong in MCP, and give authors a reliable place to present SEPs, ext-auth drafts, prototypes, and deployment results for cross-topic feedback. The charter defines the scope; discussion and rough consensus happen in one channel and one recurring call, and the work products are drafts and demos rather than new standing groups.

title: Authorization Charter
content: Deployment experience reports: how implementers have integrated the current authorization spec (OAuth 2.1, RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata, RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration, Client ID Metadata Documents) with real authorization servers, and where it falls short Extension interoperability reports: results of pairing independent implementations of the ext-auth extensions end to end (for example IdP, client, and authorization server through the Enterprise-Managed Authorization ID-JAG exchange), including IdP capability gaps, workarounds, and conformance scenario input Enterprise identity integration: requirements and friction points when connecting MCP servers to enterprise IdPs (Okta, Entra ID, Ping, Keycloak, etc.), including SSO, tenant isolation, and admin consent flows Delegated and agentic access: use cases for on-behalf-of token exchange, downstream resource access, audience restriction, and consent when an MCP client acts through chains of agents or tools Scope and permission granularity: whether and how MCP servers should advertise fine-grained scopes (per-tool, per-resource) and how clients should request and present them, and authorization granularity beyond scope strings (Rich Authorization Requests, structured denials, remediation hints) Credentials for non-HTTP transports: patterns for stdio, WebSocket, and future transports where the HTTP authorization spec does not directly apply Client identity and registration: operator experience with Dynamic Client Registration, Client ID Metadata Documents, software statements, and pre-registered clients Threat modelling input: cataloguing authorization-related attack surfaces (token confusion, confused-deputy, audience mismatch, redirect handling) to inform Security Best Practices documentation SEP and draft feedback: authorization-related SEPs, ext-auth drafts, reference implementations, and demos are presented on the call and in #auth-ig threads for feedback before and during the SEP process; the IG’s

title: Authorization Charter
content: IG’s rough consensus is recorded in meeting notes for sponsors and Core Maintainers to draw on Problem statements and requirements: use-case catalogues and recommendations shared in #auth-ig threads and on SEP pull requests for consumption by SEP authors

title: Authorization Charter
content: Accepting SEPs or extensions: the IG gives feedback and signals support; sponsorship and acceptance follow the SEP guidelines and remain with Maintainers and Core Maintainers Authentication of end users to MCP clients: how a host application authenticates its own users is a host concern, not a protocol concern Transport security (TLS, mTLS, certificate handling): belongs to the Transports WG Server identity, provenance, and trust signalling: belongs to the Server Card / Registry efforts End-user product configuration walk-throughs: the IG discusses patterns, not step-by-step setup for individual IdP products. Vendor-reported constraints on what an authorization server or IdP can or cannot implement are in scope as deployment experience Competitively sensitive or non-public business information, per the MCP Antitrust Policy

title: Authorization Charter
content: Security IG: token-audience confusion, issuer validation, and account-linking risks sit at the boundary between the two groups Transports WG: authorization is currently specified at the HTTP transport level; changes to transports affect where credentials are carried Agents IG: delegated/on-behalf-of access and consent for multi-agent chains overlap heavily with agentic use cases Server Card WG / Registry: client and server identity, discovery metadata, and trust establishment intersect with how authorization servers and resource servers are located and verified SDK Maintainers: SDKs ship the auth client implementations; IG findings should inform cross-SDK auth ergonomics and defaults

title: Authorization Charter
content: Open to anyone; no formal membership or approval step is required to join the channel, attend calls, or contribute. The group particularly seeks identity-provider vendors, MCP client and server implementers shipping authorization support, and operators integrating MCP with enterprise IdPs. Join the #auth-ig channel on the MCP Contributors Discord and start or join a thread for your topic. Calls are open and attendance is optional — async participation in Discord threads is equally valued.

title: Authorization Charter
content: Meeting Frequency Duration Purpose Auth IG Call Every 2 weeks 45 min Agenda-driven: problem pitches, SEP and draft progress, demos, deployment reports Discord: #auth-ig

title: Authorization Charter
content: All authorization discussion happens in #auth-ig, with one Discord thread per topic (for example a SEP number, a draft name, or a deployment pairing). There are no per-topic channels. Meeting agendas and notes live in the channel’s per-call agenda thread, with a link cross-posted to GitHub Discussions as the group governance rules require.

title: Authorization Charter
content: The call keeps a fixed biweekly slot, but each meeting is built from its agenda: A facilitator opens an agenda thread in #auth-ig ahead of each call. Anyone may request a slot by replying with the topic, the ask (feedback, decision, awareness), and the time needed. Facilitators agree the agenda and hand out time slots before the call. If the agenda is thin, the call is cancelled in the thread and the slot is kept for next time. Typical slots are a problem pitch, a progress update on a SEP or ext-auth draft, a demo of a prototype or reference implementation, or a deployment or interoperability report from implementers of a shipped extension.

title: Authorization Charter
content: Two standing questions are asked of every problem pitch before anyone invests in a SEP: Is this a problem worth solving? Is there real deployment demand, and is the gap in the protocol rather than in one product? Does it belong here? Is the right home the core specification, an official extension in ext-auth, an unofficial extension, or an upstream standards body? When the answer to both is yes, the proposer drafts a SEP or ext-auth pull request through the normal SEP process, finds a sponsor, and returns to the call to present progress and demos as the draft matures. The IG does not charter a sub-group, channel, or meeting series per topic. Contributors who already meet separately on a topic are welcome to keep doing so, and bring outcomes back to the call as agenda slots. A separate Working Group can still be proposed through the standard process when a deliverable genuinely needs its own decision rights, but that is the exception rather than the default path.

title: Authorization Charter
content: The IG’s outputs are the drafts and demos that pass through it: authorization SEPs and ext-auth specifications with recorded IG feedback, reference implementations and conformance scenarios, interoperability and deployment reports, and published meeting notes. The IG stewards modelcontextprotocol/ext-auth, where authorization extension specifications land via PR. Success looks like authorization proposals reaching Core Maintainer review with cross-topic feedback already incorporated, and shipped extensions accumulating independent interoperable implementations.

content: Charter for the MCP Enterprise Interest Group.

title: Enterprise Interest Group Charter
content: Interest Group

title: Enterprise Interest Group Charter
content: The Enterprise IG identifies and documents the requirements gaps that enterprises encounter when deploying MCP in production. As MCP adoption scales across regulated industries and large organizations, enterprise teams face recurring gaps in areas such as authentication integration, identity propagation, audit and compliance, gateway behavior, scalability and resilience, and configuration management that are not yet addressed at the protocol level. The group brings together enterprise practitioners to capture these gaps as problem statements and structured recommendations, and to channel them to the relevant Working Groups for specification work. Governance and best-practice patterns may emerge from these discussions, but the group’s core mandate is surfacing protocol-level requirements, not maintaining a general best-practices catalog. All discussions and sessions are protocol-focused and vendor-neutral. The Enterprise IG is not a venue for product pitches or vendor-specific marketing. Participants contribute as practitioners sharing deployment experience and requirements, not as representatives promoting commercial solutions.

title: Enterprise Interest Group Charter
content: Enterprise Requirements Gaps (overarching focus): The group’s primary mandate is identifying enterprise deployment requirements that are not addressed at the MCP protocol level today and turning them into problem statements and recommendations for the relevant Working Groups. Each requirement is captured with the enterprise opportunity it represents, not only the pain point, since closing these gaps is what unlocks broader enterprise adoption and value. The specific domains below are explored through that lens; governance and best-practice patterns are documented only where they surface a protocol-level gap: Enterprise Authentication and Identity: Discussion of enterprise-managed auth patterns including IdP integration (SSO, SAML, OIDC), token lifecycle management, On-Behalf-Of (OBO) token exchange flows, and fine-grained authorization (Rich Authorization Requests). Gathering requirements to inform the Authorization IG and related SEPs. Identity Propagation and Session Context: Defines how verified identity is surfaced and conveyed across MCP clients, servers, and downstream services for policy enforcement and audit. This includes spawned-agent and delegated-agent use cases: identity lineage, least-privilege for child agents, descendant revocation, and auditability across multi-agent chains, which is adjacent to authentication but distinct in focus. Audit, Observability, and Compliance: Exploration of standardized audit trail formats for MCP tool invocations, integration with enterprise SIEM and observability platforms, and evidence generation for compliance frameworks (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, EU AI Act). Includes sector-specific compliance patterns such as PHI handling and BAA-scoped data flows in healthcare environments. Gateway and Proxy Behavior: Documentation of enterprise deployment patterns where MCP traffic routes through API gateways, load balancers, reverse proxies, and security proxies. With the move to a stateless protocol core in the 2026-07-28 release, the

title: Enterprise Interest Group Charter
content: the focus shifts from session affinity to gaps that persist in a stateless model: header and context propagation, authorization handoff across proxies, and policy enforcement at the gateway. Scalability and Resilience: Running MCP at enterprise scale across regions and availability zones. With the stateless core enabling horizontal scaling without sticky sessions, the focus is on failover, load distribution, and reliability for mission-critical deployments. MCP in Enterprise Architecture: Definition of how MCP fits into broader enterprise architecture, including integration with existing middleware, data platforms, and agent orchestration layers. Configuration Portability and Deployment: Discussion of challenges in deploying MCP servers across heterogeneous client environments, multi-tenant configuration patterns, and enterprise-scale rollout practices. Interceptors and Middleware: Exploration of use cases for request/response interception in MCP pipelines, including PII redaction, compliance validation, content filtering, and hallucination detection. Gathering requirements that may inform future specification work on middleware patterns. Problem Statements and Use Cases: Documentation of enterprise pain points and production failure scenarios (anonymized) to build an evidence base for prioritizing specification work. Recommendations to Working Groups: Providing structured input from enterprise practitioners to the Authorization IG, Security IG, Gateways IG, and other groups on enterprise-specific requirements.

title: Enterprise Interest Group Charter
content: Writing or owning SEPs. The Enterprise IG produces problem statements, use cases, and recommendations. Concrete specification changes are driven through the appropriate Working Groups. Discussion of product-specific or vendor-specific solutions. Discussions must remain vendor-neutral and focused on protocol-level patterns. General MCP support or onboarding. The group focuses on enterprise deployment challenges, not introductory MCP topics. Overlapping directly with the Authorization IG’s specification work. The Enterprise IG gathers enterprise auth requirements and feeds them to the Authorization IG rather than proposing auth protocol changes.

title: Enterprise Interest Group Charter
content: Working Groups Transports WG — Transport-level needs for enterprise support (non-functional requirements such as latency and horizontal scaling) are bundled and provided as input to the Transports WG. Extensions WG — Requirements for extensions other than authorization are bundled and provided as input to the Extensions WG. Interest Groups Authorization IG — Enterprise auth requirements (IdP integration, OBO flows, RAR) are gathered and provided as input to the Authorization IG’s specification work. Security IG — Overlapping interest in runtime security, tool poisoning, and credential management. The Enterprise IG focuses on the organizational and governance dimensions; the Security IG focuses on threat models and protocol-level mitigations. Gateways IG — Direct overlap on gateway/proxy behavior patterns. The Enterprise IG provides enterprise deployment context; the Gateways IG focuses on technical gateway specifications. Financial Services IG — Several enterprise concerns (compliance, audit, regulated environments) overlap with the FS-IG. Cross-posting and joint sessions will be coordinated where appropriate.
